speechtext: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON COMMEMORATION OF 25th ANNIVERSARY OF END OF SECOND WORLD WAR

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Eudes Dube (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members are doubtless aware that next May 8 is the 25th anniversary of the end of World War II in Europe. In this connection, I would like to announce to the House the Government's plans to commemorate this occasion. It marks a great moment in Canadian history, as Canadians played an illustrious part in the events leading to this day of liberation for the Old World in 1945.
May the eighth this year falls on a Friday. The Government plans to hold a colourful and impressive ceremony that evening on Parliament Hill. Veterans of World War II 21701-31
and their present-day counterparts will participate. They will lead the country in paying homage to the 44,893 Canadian men and women who sacrificed their fives in the bitter five-year struggle to preserve freedom in Europe and in the world. We are hoping the people of the national capital region will want to take part in the occasion personally and that the people of Canada will be able to share in it via television and radio. Maybe the young people of Canada will feel a more intense pride in their country if they become involved in this simple, moving ceremony of remembrance in the shadow of the Peace Tower.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
However, we have not planned to hold only a memorial service. Those members of the House who recall May 8, 1945-and especially those who were serving their country at the time-will remember the wild wave of jubilation that surged through the hearts of free men everywhere in the world. The wistful words of one of the most poignant songs of the war had come true. The fights had gone on again all over the world.
So we hope our proposed VE-day ceremony on Parliament Hill will also close on a note of thanksgiving and hope.
I might add, Mr. Speaker, that various local and national ceremonies will be held in Western Europe this spring, and in cases where Canada has been invited to take part we will be suitably represented and announcements in this regard will be made from time to time.
We are not aware of any inter-allied ceremonies scheduled for this time in Europe. However, if we were to be invited by any of our World War II allies to participate in their commemoration ceremonies, I am sure the House would want Canada to play its part, with the enthusiasm and dedication v/hich helped create the original Victory-in-Europe Day.
The House can be confident, Mr. Speaker, that it will be advised if any such interallied plans should develop.

Mr. Speaker, I feel it a distinct
3816	COMMONS
Commemoration of World War II honour to comment on the minister's announcement of the government's intention to commemorate on May 8 the 25th anniversary of the end of World War II in Europe. The commemoration of this historic event, while it will give us an opportunity to pay homage to the 45,000 Canadian men and women who lost their lives in war, will also remind us,
I hope, of our duty as citizens of this great dominion to reflect on those veterans who, although they offered their lives, still remain with us and are reaching the twilight years of their lives incapacitated and dependent on those who lead the nation and are responsible to provide the proper care which these people deserve.
In our present world of strife and turmoil, and even with the evidence of apparent problems which Canadians face at this very moment, not the least of which is our striving for national unity, I hope this anniversary will remind us of the reasons we have become a great nation. Those men and women who died on the battlefield, together with those of us who remain, fought side by side as comrades regardless of race, creed or colour and defended the free world and their own nation against one of the greatest tyrannies in the history of mankind, not as different religious groups looking for preference in our society but in the same colour uniform, as Canadians.
I hope the services planned for this significant memorial will not only bring representation and participation of veterans from across our great dominion, but will also bring together in a spirit of comradeship those of us who represent different political philosophies as a declaration of unity in remembering those veterans who gave us the freedom to govern all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, let me first of all congratulate the minister for setting up suitable ceremonies to help us celebrate the 25th anniversary of the end of the second world war. I appreciate that arrangements for certain of the ceremonies which will be held by some of the nations which fought in that war have not been completed yet. We look forward to Canada being represented in that community of nations in a suitable manner and by suitable veterans.
Canadian servicemen and women made a great contribution to victory in that war. Let us really show our appreciation as a nation by increasing war veterans pensions and al-

DEBATES	February 19, 1970
lowances in order to demonstrate our regard for the sacrifices they made on behalf of us all.
Hear, hear.

After 25 years, almost 50 per cent of our population does not remember the last war. This will surprise many of us. It throws an extra task on those who have the responsibility for looking after the veterans of that war; they must explain to the nation the reason that war was fought, and draw attention to the sacrifices which were made by Canadian men and women to establish peace, as they hoped, for all time.
Peace cannot be established by pacifism. We must be willing to fight for it and make sacrifices for it.
Hear, hear.

If these ceremonies are to be truly representative of the Canadian nation we shall have to tell the young people of Canada that though war is a disaster for everyone there are times when it is absolutely necessary in order to ensure the peace which we all desire. It seems that many people across the world have forgotten this in terms of the United Nations and the reason it was set up. Part of our responsibility in the course of these ceremonies must be to inform our young people of the reasons for the sacrifices made by our veterans and to remind them of our responsibility to make those veterans who remain with us comfortable in the remaining days of their lives.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, we derive great pride from our contribution to the defence of liberty in Europe. However, we grieve for the 44,893 Canadian men and women who lost their lives thereby. It was indeed somewhat ridiculous that a small population should have sent a few thousand of its citizens to defend millions of people. Our technical and financial assistance should have been enough. We can remember the famous plebiscite on conscription which fully support my opinion.
I have no desire to minimize the value of the heroic deeds of those Canadians who made the sacrifice of their lives. I do, however, want to express the wish, on this anniversary, that a similar effort be made, but this time for peace.
February 19, 1970
Hear, hear.

The funds and the production which helped us to win the war would also certainly have created the peace we all long to see prevail throughout the world.
The Social Credit methods applied in wartime can just as well apply in times of peace.
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Eric Kierans (Postmaster General and Minisler of Communications):
speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Postmaster General
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL POSTAL CODING SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make an announcement concerning the Post Office's plans with regard to a national postal code, and at the same time, to table copies in both languages of a report titled, "A Canadian Public Address Postal Coding System".
As hon. members will recall, last July the Post Office engaged the consulting firm of Samson Belair Riddell Stead Inc. to carry out a study of a possible national postal code. Their report was completed last December and as a result we intend to implement a national public address postal code.
Several countries now use, or plan to use postal codes, among them the United States, Britain, Germany and Japan. The code which has been designed for Canada will be unique. It will provide great flexibility, precision, and be able to accommodate changes in population distribution.
21701-31J
Montreal Post Office Strike
[English}
The code itself will consist of six alphabetical and numerical characters. The first three characters will be used for forward sortation, that is, they will describe the area to which the letter is being sent. As an example-and this is purely an example-the address code of a letter mailed to a customer in Scarborough, Ontario, could begin with the letter "T" to designate the Toronto coding region and be followed by the numerals 8 and 7 to designate both Scarborough and the appropriate postal station. The last three characters of the six-character code will describe the local delivery unit, which might be an apartment building a street block and so on.
Implementing the code will take time and a considerable amount of work. Detailed planning will commence very shortly. Discussions will be held between officers of the department and interested groups across the country with the object of ensuring that the code, as finally designed, will meet as many customer requirements as possible. These meetings will begin shortly.
The basic design of the national code will be completed by November, 1970. Implementation will begin with a detailed pilot project scheduled to start in April, 1971. A period of testing and analysis will be followed by implementation in other cities. Ottawa is likely to be chosen as the test site because the new postal terminal due to be opened here this summer will include facilities to test new models of equipment, thus enabling us to examine the performance of the code under existing as well as future conditions.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the staff of the Canada Post Office on the speed with which this particular project has moved and on the scope of the task that they have undertaken. A permanent public address code will be a major factor both in increasing the productivity of the Post Office and in improving the quality of service which we will be able to provide the public.
The national code will entail an upgrading of job skills in Post Office and bring about a reduction in the number of routine tasks. Before the code goes into effect, there will be full consultations with the different unions or associations representing employees concerned.

It can be said, however, that despite the brilliance of the press release this is not a trail-blazing experiment because, as the statement points out, many countries are already using zipcodes and there is not, so far as I can learn, complete unanimity as to the efficacy of this particular device. As one of my colleagues in front of me has just observed, the public has been zapped and now the Post Office is being zipped.
It can be said, however, and we want to analyse these announcements-I think that is our job, Mr. Speaker-that considering the ills of the Post Office, aggravated in the last two years by the minister's brash, brusque and bull headed efforts at reform, the introduction of a zipcode can hardly be considered as a major remedial measure. Mr. Speaker, on the ground of urgent and pressing necessity I ask unanimous consent of the House to move a motion based on the following facts. More than 879 Indians and Metis families in northern Saskatchewan are faced with starvation. They need help from any available source. Yet, when members of the Saskatchewan Farmers' Union as long ago as December were prepared to make available to them several thousand bushels of wheat, the Indian and Metis families were prohibited by Wheat Board regulations from making any use of this humanitarian offer. These people live under extremely adverse conditions and the government must move quickly to help them. I move:
That the government immediately take such measures as are necessary by law to permit the members of the Saskatchewan Farmers' Union to give several thousand bushels of wheat to Metis families in northern Saskatchewan and to permit the MStis committee of Saskatoon to make lawful arrangements to grist such grain and distribute the flour to the starving Metis and their families.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. In view of the statement made yesterday by President Nixon in his foreign policy speech to Congress that "the most pressing issue regarding the law of the sea is the need to achieve agreement on the breadth of the territorial sea, to head off the escalating national claims over the ocean", will the government now proclaim Canada's sovereignty over our Arctic waters in clear, unmistakable terms so that we do not lose that sovereignty by default because of our continued silence on this matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ARCTIC WATERS-STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT NIXON-DECLARATION OF CANADIAN POSITION

Mr. Speaker, if I may be permitted to answer the question put by the hon. gentleman, let me say that we do not claim sovereignty over any waters that have been regarded as the high seas, except possibly where there has been an extension of territorial waters or inland waters as the result of the application of straight baselines.
February 19, 1970	COMMONS
It would be difficult to argue that the Arctic waters between Canadian territory have been regarded as part of the high seas. Indeed, the experimental voyage of the Manhattan in our waters, conducted with our acquiescence and our co-operation, is evidence to the contrary. So the President of the United States could not have been referring to Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the terms of this motion are that this House concur in the report of the committee. The committee, under its terms of reference, was ordered to consider and report on the problems of the dairy industry referred to it for study.
Now, there can be no objection to the manner in which the committee considered these matters. I believe the committee did so ably and well. There can be no objection to the recommendations of the committee; they
DEBATES	3831
Government Dairy Policy should be concurred in by this House and implemented by the government. That which is objectionable is the ineptness of the language used to express the committee's second recommendation. The language does not state a clear recommendation which, if concurred in by the House, would define in terms certain a course of action which the government could implement or refuse to implement.
The recommendation presently reads:
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Your Committee recommends:
2. Having regard for the disruption in the industry which may be caused by a decrease in the funds available for the dairy support programs, your Committee urges in the strongest possible terms that the Government consider maintaining the dairy support programs at the 1969-70 level for the period 1970-71, namely $125,000,000.
In a few minutes I intend to move an amendment which would correct the wording of this recommendation. I should like to explain some of the reasons. Here we have the words "Your Committee" repeated as the subject of a sentence. Obviously, once is enough. Then we find the word "recommends" followed by the word "urges". If both words are left in, some hon. members might be concurring in the word "recommends" and others in the word "urges". Since the committee was empowered to recommend but not empowered to "urge", the word "urge" must be taken out.
Next we have the phrase "in the strongest possible terms". What are these strong terms? The words are subjective. They invite each member of the House to apply the descriptive adverbs to the word "recommend" which each believes are the strongest adverbs that can be used. I suggest it is for the committee itself to supply these strongest possible terms so that members of the House can concur in or dissent from them. I may say that the recommendation is not expressed in the strongest possible terms and thus belies itself. To ask the government to "consider" maintaining the present level of dairy price supports does not involve the use of strong terms. There is nothing constitutionally wrong with recommending that the government maintain these price supports. Such a recommendation does not offend either section 54 of the B.N.A. Act or Standing Order 62; such a recommendation does not purport to appropriate any public revenue. To "urge that the government consider" is to subvert the committee's consensus that the recommendation be "in the strongest possible terms".

The terms of reference do not confine the committee to any over-all sums aEotted to specific purposes or programs. The phrasing of the terms of reference includes the words "the funds available for dairy support in the forthcoming year". The "forthcoming year", I suggest, means the year commencing April 1, 1970 and ending March 31, 1971. Quite obviously, any sums mentioned as available in that period are hypothetical and will not be fixed untU finally voted upon on third reading of the appropriations biU. Even the estimates, as their name suggests, are not final. The House had a recent illustration of this fact in the tabling of revised estimates for the year 1968-69.
The phrase "funds available in the forthcoming year" also includes those amounts that may be added by way of a supplementary supply bill. Since the phrase "funds available for dairy support in the forthcoming year" refers to hypothetical amounts, any recommendation by the committee as to the amount of the funds would also be hypothetical. In the same way, any statement by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) as to the amounts that will be available for each program is a reference to amounts that are hypothetical. The words do not mean any more coming from the minister than from any other member of the House until the estimates are voted upon and passed.
There are many other problems in the dairy industry. I had the opportunity of attending a meeting yesterday with 500 dairymen, and there is great concern in the industry. I could go on and refer to many aspects of the industry, but my time is limited. I suggest that if the original recommendation No. 2 is acceptable to the House-and it appears to be-then the amendment that I am proposing to move should also be accepted by the House. Therefore, I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Joliette <Mr. La Salle):
That the report be referred back to the committee with an instruction to so revise the second recommendation of the report by correction of grammar and deletion of surplus wordage as to express clearly the consensus of the committee, that the committee having regard for the disruption in the industry which may be caused by a decrease in the funds available for the dairy price support programs strongly recommends that the government maintain the dairy price support programs in the forthcoming year at the sum of $125 million, and that the committee report back to this House by February 26, 1970.

May I first draw Your Honour's attention to Standing Order 62, to which the hon. member has also referred. I submit the terms of this Standing Order are clear. It provides:
This House shall not adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue-
I do not need to read further since I suggest it is clear that any wording in a committee report that could form the substance of a motion, which in turn would be voted upon and made a decision of the House, is out of order unless the motion is moved upon the recommendation of the Governor General. That, of course, is not possible in view of what my hon. friend has said.
May I also draw to your attention citation 260 of Beauchesne's fourth edition which provides:
The tendency has been in the Canadian House of Commons, for the past twenty-five years, to rule out all motions purporting to give the government a direct order to do a thing which cannot be done without the expenditure of money.
The citation goes on to provide in paragraph (3):
A motion to refer to a Select Committee a Return to an Address respecting a claim for damages against the Government is in order, but the House could not concur in a report from the committee recommending payment, without the previous recommendation of the Crown.
I think that makes the situation clear. There are other citations I should Eke to draw to your attention. For example, citation 278 on page 227 of Beauchesne's fourth edition provides:
(3) Reductions can be made in Committee on the Bill, but no grant can be increased except upon recommendation of the Crown.

Further, I draw your attention to citation 288, which provides, in part:
Committees are regarded as portions of the House and are governed for the most part in their proceedings by the same rules which prevail in the House.
I submit it is very clear that no member of this House, other than a member of the government, can move a motion, the adoption of which would result in the expenditure of funds from the public treasury, no matter how small in amount. This House has decided that the total substance of a standing committee's report to this House can become the subject of a motion, and that motion is the motion for concurrence in the committee's report to this House. If the House decides to concur in a standing committee's report, then, of course, the report becomes a decision of the House.
It is clearly out of order for any member of the House, other than a member of the government, to move a motion, the passage of which would have the effect of making a charge on the public treasury.
The hon. member argued that the estimates for the coming fiscal year, 1970-71, are not determined at this point, since all that has happened is that they have been laid before the House in the form of the blue book. Even agreeing with that, it must be clear that no member, except a member of the government, has the right to move a motion in the House that will increase or establish the level of certain expenditures, whether adopted by the House or not.

Mr. Speaker, the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Agriculture is moving today a motion for concurrence in the report of the proceedings of the committee, according to an order of the House passed on December 18.
The committee held meetings and heard representatives from several associations of dairy producers. Today, the conclusions of the report are submitted to us.
It will be recalled that in May and June of last year, a special study was undertaken on, among other things, the same problem and matter now before us. But then, the committee travelled extensively in the eastern part of Canada, in order to determine the consequences of the dairy policy of the federal government.
The conclusions of this report, which involved a large expenditure of public funds, are contradictory, in the view of the very members of the committee who made the study trip. We find ourselves in a somewhat embarrassing and paradoxical situation, for, on the one hand, we are in possession of the recommendations of a study which had to be completed by February 17 and, on the other hand, we do not have at our disposal the recommendations originating from a more thorough study that was performed on the same subject.
The chairman of the Committee on Agriculture claimed, a little earlier, that he cannot submit the recommendations contained in the study carried on in May and June last, because the terms of reference were to study the general situation of agriculture in Canada.
Hon. members know that the dairy policy is usually announced on April 1. Now today, the
February 19, 1970

Government Dairy Policy House has to decide whether to concur in the report of the committee on that dairy policy, but it does not have the much more relevant and important conclusions of a more exhaustive study which will be presented to the House much later than April 1.
Thus the government is asking the House to concur in the conclusions of a report without stating at the same time all the aspects which have been the subject-matter of expert studies made at public expense. The House cannot concur in an incomplete report, if it really wants what is good for the dairy producers concerned.
That is where we stand as members of Parliament. Today, we are going to adopt a report of the committee on the dairy policy. On April 1 next, the government, through the Minister of Agriculture, will state its dairy policy and it is to be expected that it will not be substantially different from this year's policy, except that the subsidies paid to the dairy industry will be reduced by $10 million, which will make matters worse for the producers.

The policy will have been adopted, and the expenses incurred for this special study "in the field", as the producers say, will have been in vain because the government's policy will already be in force.

That is why I had agreed on December 18 last to give unanimous consent, provided however that the findings of the study made in May and June be printed as an appendix to this report.
If the chairman of the Standing Committee on Agriculture really wants to help Quebec dairy farmers, he has to admit that we are right on that point.
It is our bounden duty to look into every aspect of the question before the announcement of the forthcoming dairy policy which is to come into effect next April 1st. It is still time to do it.
There is still a month and a half before April 1st, which leaves us plenty of time to draft the findings of the study made last May

It is easy to find all kind of excuses, Listening to the chairman of the committee a few minutes ago, we were aware of the awkwardness of his position, of his embarrassment in the presence of the dairy producers who are with us here and of the inconsistency between what he does and what he says.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-INSUFFICIENCY OF GOVERNMENT DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
That this House condemns the Government policy on the dairy industry
1.	For having stated its dairy policy for 1969-70 at the very last moment, namely on March 31, 1969, and not having taken into account recommendations from producers concerned;
2.	For having contributed to reducing the dairy producers' income by cutting down the subsidies and increasing the export tax;
3.	For having listed in the 1970-71 Estimates a reduction in the dairy industry subsidies, which will further reduce the dairy producers' income.
Mr. Speaker, first I should like to thank all those who have been instrumental in allowing us to have as much time as possible to examine in an objective manner the very special problem of the dairy industry.
Everyone will certainly agree that the dairy industry is going through difficult times. However there is no such agreement when it comes to having the dairy producers alone carry the load. We remember quite well that a few years ago federal as well as provincial authorities invited the dairy producers to modernize their farms, to increase their herds, so that they might produce enough to meet the market requirements and to make their business more economical, which was the only way to get better prices.
Now this is what the Minister of Agriculture said in this House on March 23, 1966:
Unless the producer's confidence in his ability to make a decent living from dairy farming is restored, we face the prospect of shortages.
In an answer given the same day, the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) made the following comments which I think were appropriate:
The minister indicated that the government was motivated first of all by the large number of dairy farmers who are going out of the dairy industry into other production such as hogs and beef. He also said he -was disturbed by the number of dairy
3838	COMMONS
Government Dairy Policy
farmers who have moved out of farming altogether to the point where Canada now faces the prospect of a severe shortage of dairy products for our own home consumption.
In my opinion, it is too painful an experience to go through before the government takes positive measures to remedy the causes. When I say it is a bit too late, I am sure the Minister of Agriculture will admit it, because thousands of dairy farmers have been gravely wronged before he made this statement.
Now, after 1966, the dairy policy was announced a little too late to benefit the producers.
In 1967, because of the seriousness of the situation and the failure of the goverment to recognize that dairy farmers were entitled to an additional income and that, in order to be in a position to meet the requirements of the Canadian market, they needed higher prices, a huge delegation turned up on Parliament Hill. That was on May 15, 1967, and the then Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) and the then Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) came and talked to the producers. This is what they told them: "You are right to come here; you should have come ten years ago, but what can we do? It would take millions of dollars." Then, the farmers went home with a solemn promise that from then on, farming policies would be long term policies drawn up along such lines as to enable dairy farmers to know which way to go.
Mr. Speaker, the organization of milk production has grown bigger. Without buying land, industrial producers did manage to increase the production of their herds through improved farming methods and selection of cow herds. Producers had an output of 150,000 pounds of milk in 1967-68, but they were able to reach 200,000 pounds in 1968-69 and production is expected to remain at that level in 1969-70. Unfortunately, their efforts are penalized by the decision of the Canadian Dairy Commission. Indeed, since quotas for this category of producers have not been increased, they do not receive any subsidies for part of their production, and they will also have to pay the levy of 52 cents per hundredweight in order to finance the exportation of milk powder. This is why a fair number of producers will incur losses of several hundreds of dollars for the year 1969-70.
I do not know how the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) in his statement of March 31 on the dairy policy of the government, could hold the support level of prices at $4.85 per hundredweight, when the current market price is $3.60 at the factory. By adding the

DEBATES	February 19, 1970
$1.25 subsidy, we get $4.85. Once the 26 cents export tax is subtracted, the actual price to the producer will be $4.59 at the factory or $4.34 at the farm. The price applies to the volume of the production included in the quota. The surplus will sell at $3.13 per hundredweight.
The former Minister of Agriculture once said that the export taxes are not payments from the State but rather taxes collected from the producer. Regarding the dairy policy of the current year, the situation is serious because some producers will hardly get $3.13 per hundredweight for part of their production. This is less than the production costs, which will likely reduce the price of the annual production of a farm.
The Minister of Agriculture would willingly answer me that if there is a production surplus, some steps should be taken to reduce it. I will reply that there is no production surplus, but rather a phenomenon of under-consumption.
According to the fifth report of the Economic Council of Canada-a government organization-one Canadian out of five is poverty-stricken. In Montreal alone, for example, thousands of families are destitute. Many children have never drunk milk, according to a survey and to an official paper sent to me with a letter by the F.C.U. Federations. This document contains some quite interesting statistics. In conclusion it says that in the city of Montreal, there are 105,800 poverty-stricken families, or 55.6 per cent of the population, and that 1,062,000 people in greater Montreal earn less than $5,000 per annum.
In view of such convincing figures, how could one formally deny the existence of a real phenomenon of under-consumption? The people who happen to live in such circumstances cannot even buy the necessities of life because they lack adequate purchasing power.
A Senate special committee was appointed to ascertain whether there really were poor people in Canada. As the House will remember, the said committee discovered that there were some and feared an uprising on their part. A release to that effect was broadcast on radio and published in the press.
I know that one of the goals of the Canadian Dairy Commission is to maintain a national dairy policy and to establish a sound, healthy and viable industry. We agree on that point. Dairy operations are to be made viable with respect to their extent and their output,
February 19, 1970	COMMONS
through quotas and subsidies, and by continuously offering to consumers an adequate supply of dairy products of high quality, at prices which, with the necessary subsidies, will provide qualified producers with a reasonable profit.
It is for that reason that a petition has been tabled in the House. It bore the signatures of
25,000	producers. The objective has not been reached, and that is precisely the subject-matter of this debate.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The volume of production must be maintained at the consumption level, the latter being conditioned at the present time by the purchasing power of people in easy circumstances. In Canada, there could be a greater consumption of dairy products if people who have needs to satisfy but lack the financial means for so doing had a greater purchasing power.
The increase in the number of unemployed, of strikes of all kinds and of taxes are the direct causes of the decreasing purchasing power of a great number of producers.
If all Canadians could purchase more dairy products, there would be hardly, if any, surplus. Can the Minister of Agriculture say and mean that all Canadians cannot consume more dairy products? Would it be impossible to sell more of them on our domestic market if an effort was made in that direction?
Through his dairy policy, the government wants to oblige the farmers to reduce their milk production. But, to reach this goal, he brings down the subsidy from $1.31 to $1.25, he increases the export tax by 5 cents on the quantity subsidized and by 520 on the surplus quota and the result of this will be to widen the gap between the selling price and the production cost. Thus the net income which is already very low will drop further.
I am quite aware that it would be better if the consumer himself were to pay an adequate price, allowing the dairy producers to clear a net profit at least equal to the gains of people involved in other sectors of the economy.
The problem is no doubt known to the Minister of Agriculture since only three years ago he told the House that the basic problem facing agriculture and all those involved in it is that the price scale is too low. Programs to increase it must be implemented. I agree entirely with the minister, but the prices should at least reach a level permitting profits in keeping with the needs of the people involved. When a ladder is too short to reach
DEBATES	3839
Government Dairy Policy the roof of a building, even if five rungs are added when ten would be needed, it will still be impossible to reach the objective. According to the new dairy policy for 1969, far from having added rungs, the government has taken a few out, as far as the farmers' income is concerned.
When the minister was a member of the opposition-and I ask him to excuse me for reminding him-he had quite different ideas. Now, we are considering a very important matter and I suggest that we examine our present and former positions.
Operation costs are increasing while incomes are declining. This was found out a long time ago by many who are well informed about agriculture in the constituencies.
Mr. Speaker, I have consulted many milk producers so as to establish quite accurately the production cost of milk per hundredweight in our province. And, among them, there is at least one who has won a medal for excellence in that field. This means that there is an accounting system on that farm and that the herd has been improved. Yet, the cost of production is $4.88 per hundredweight at the plant, labour included.
For the information of hon. members who would like to know exactly what it costs to produce 100 pounds of milk and what operations are necessary to ensure the smooth running of a farm so that they may be in a position to judge if really all these dairy producers who are in the galleries today and who have signed a petition are right, I will give a few figures.
And once they hear the statistics which I am to give them presently, I am quite sure that they will agree that farmers and industrial milk producers do not get their fair share of the national revenue, and that they cannot live adequately in this just society which is yet to come.
Let us take the case of a farmer who produces 218,000 pounds of milk. He is not a small farmer who produces 12,000 pounds. I know him pretty well. I saw him start when he was young. He is married now and is bringing up his small family. He has done well and is hoping to do even better. When he started he had in mind a nice dairy farm where he would produce milk of quality in order to meet the needs of the market.
I will tell hon. members what his expenses were, which no doubt will be of interest to them. How much did it cost him in 1968-69
3840	COMMONS
Government Dairy Policy for feed? Exactly $2,358.15. For fertilizer? $984.06. For seed? $288.06. For the purchase of cattle and for artificial insemination? $536.00. For wages paid? $275.00. For tractor maintenance? $376.82. For hay, green oats, etc. $960.00. For truck maintenance? $327.01. For land maintenance? $121.30. For machinery maintenance? There is no exaggeration here: $59.05. For interest, taxes and insurance? $767.21. For family requirements? $324.70. For transportation? $538.92. For miscellaneous farm expenses? $365.70. For tractor and other work given by contract? $436.25. For capital expenditures? $139.00. For 10 per cent depreciation on machinery? $640.00. For 5 per cent depreciation on farm buildings? $278.40. Total expenses amount to $9,776.25.
As for receipts, he sold some wood which he cut on his farm for $75.48, cattle for $2,000 and milk for $7,675.91; he received subsidies amounting to $2,676.42. As for his non-farm income-he is also a carpenter-it amounted to $459.69. He had therefore an income of $12,887.50 and he showed a net profit of $3,111.25. He worked 3,000 hours and his wife 800 hours. The hourly wage was 82 cents. A hundredweight of milk therefore cost $4.88.
Some will say that things are better elsewhere. I have in hand a document from Ontario giving the findings of a study made in 1964 on 1206 herds. The average herd was made up of 28 cows and the production by cow was 9,600 pounds. After the expenses were paid, this group of 1,200 Ontario farmers succeeded in producing milk at $4.60 per hundredweight, thus showing a profit of $48 per cow. How fantastic! The total multiplied by 30 or 35 will show the income of farmers in dairy production, a really interesting but insufficient figure.
Our figures are questioned. Everyone is very careful on that subject. At some point, the Quebec government ordered an inquiry into the conditions of agriculture in the province. It was the April Commission, though it was certainly not in the month of April. Table 15 on page 48 of the report shows the income of industrial milk producers.
To go back to the farmer I was talking about earlier, he has an average production of
8,000	pounds per cow. Let us refer to the table: for 9,000 pounds and 3,000 hours of work, the net revenue is 83 cents an hour.
It is obvious from the figures I have just quoted that the situation of dairy farmers is not very bright. Some may suggest that it

DEBATES	February 19, 1970
might be more profitable if the milk production per cow were increased.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
That formula would be ideal, for it Would bring dairy producers an income at least comparable to that of the farmers in the United States.
But what is going on in the States? In Minnesota, Michigan and Wisconsin the dairy industry is highly developed. Yet, according to the American agricultural statistics bureau, the average milk production per cow in Minnesota is 9,430 lbs., in Michigan, 9,480 lbs. and in Wisconsin, 9,600.
It is therefore obvious that there is still a long way to go to reach an average production of 12,000 lbs., even in the United States.
In Quebec there are surely herds that have reached that average. The member for Richelieu (Mr. Cote), when he was farming, may have reached an average production of
12.000	lbs. per cow, but since he has become a member of parliament there have been changes. Even with an average production of
12.000	lbs. of milk per cow, the producer of manufactured milk who depends on outside help whose working hours are limited to eight a day, cannot expect profitable operations.
I know from experience that even with the help of his wife, a farmer cannot keep a herd of over 35 milch-cowB. Have the members ever considered the amount of work involved in keeping such a herd for a full year? Indeed, more than 35 cows are needed. In addition, young cattle are required to renew the herd. All told some 50 to 60 heads may be required. This represents an average of five hours of work a day in the stable, and that, for 365 days a year. For those people, Sunday is not a day off and besides they have to sow, to make hay, to harvest their grain, to plough, to look after the pastures, to maintain the fences, the buildings and so on.
To go on with my comparison with the United States, the average price paid for manufactured milk to producers in that country in 1968 was $4.45 per hundredweight, which is absorbed by the American consumer. The price for butter is 83J cents and is also absorbed by the consumer. Fertilizers are much cheaper in the U.S. than here. In Canada, ammonium nitrate, for instance, costs $98 per ton, when in the United States it costs only $73. Superphosphate with a 45 per cent content costs $102 per ton in Quebec-when in the United States it costs $81.
February 19, 1970	COMMONS
Potassium chloride costs $71.50 compared to $49 in the United States.
Besides, the period of stabilization is shorter in the U.S.A. than in eastern Canada, which lowers further the cost of production and the cost of machinery so that farm income is higher in the United States.
In Canada, the cost of production keeps on climbing. In the past ten years the cost of fertilizers has gone up 20 per cent.
In 1949, the retail price for butter was 63 cents and in 1969 it had reached 70 or 71 cents although the price of every item needed by the farmer to produce has increased tremendously and his net income has decreased by that much.
We are sometimes reminded reproachfully that in Quebec, the capitalization per cow is too high. According to the official figures I have in hand, the average per dairy cow is $1,469 for the whole Canada, $1,616 for Ontario and $1,237 for Quebec, which shows that Quebec producers surely do not have the highest capitalization in Canada.
Prices go up in many fields: interest rates on farm loans, insurance rates, taxes, postal rates, prices of building materials, of farm machinery and salary increases in many industrial sectors as well as in the public service.
Since the dairy producers have to pay the same price as anybody else but are not given the benefit of an income that would enable them to meet the present price requirements, how can we expect them to be satisfied?
It is as though one wanted to feed a two-inch pipe with a one-inch opening. There would not be much pressure and the outflow would be rather slow. That is how it is now with the dairy producer.
There is but one area where there was a decrease, that is in the subsidy for the production of industrial milk. The objective of a just society was forgotten. Some may say there Is a limit, that the government has done enough for the farmers, who should have enough pride to live out of their production without resorting to government subsidies.
Is the dairy industry the only one receiving subsidies to survive? Not in the least. In fact, under a law passed in 1967, the subsidies granted to companies operating gold mines amounted to $15 million.
During the fiscal year 1967-68, the government has granted the companies operating coal mines in Cape Breton $25.5 million in subsidies with a view to providing jobs for
DEBATES	3841
Government Dairy Policy 4,222 workers earning $2.63 per hour for an 8-hour day as compared to 83 cents per hour, which is the salary of a farmer toiling 16 hours a day.
On June 15, 1967, the Minister of Industry. Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) said that the subsidy had been $4,000 yearly for each miner.
The government has also subsidized several companies to help them carry on and develop their business while meeting financial undertakings amounting roughly to $148 million.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I could mention companies such as Consolidated Paper which was granted a $3 million subsidy. Since we are on the subject of efficiency and subsidies, everybody knows that the Canadian National, which is administered by very able people, gets every year subsidies which enable it to straighten up its balance sheet.
I said that in 1949, the retail price of butter was 63 cents whereas skilled worker earned an average of $1.25 per hour. This means that one could get two pounds of butter for the equivalent of one hour's work whereas in 1969, according to statistics, the average salary per hour, in the same trades, could buy four pounds of butter. The ratio is higher when it applies to professional people. The farmer is always the last one to see the price of his products increase or go down. He can never see the roof because there are never enough rungs on the income scale.
To reach the price level of the other Canadian products which have increased since 1949 according to the fluctuation of the dollar, butter should sell for $1.05 on the Canadian market. Who benefited finally from the price being set at 65 cents, if not the consumer?
The ministers, the bankers, the scientists, all those who earn large salaries can benefit from the subsidy of 30 cents or 35 cents for every pound of butter, and this is what is called the compensated discount. The consumers pay less for it and the producers get the set price.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture claims that there is a surplus of dairy products, that he lowered the subsidy on industrial milk in order to curb production. The agricultural workers are really the ones who are penalized for their efficiency and for their hard work.
Yet, there is a surplus of manpower-

speechtext:
But as a government, and as responsible Members of Parliament, we have to face the facts of the situation which is now building up in the marketplace despite the best efforts of many people in the dairy industry to promote an increased sale of these products both inside Canada and abroad.

DEBATES	February 19, 1970
I agree with what the hon. member had to say about the responsibility of the government and of the Canadian Dairy Commission forgiving some advance indication to the dairy producers of what their total production ought to be. I think producers need guidance from time to time as to the market potential, and in my view this is the exact purpose for which subsidy quotas were established. A farmer knows in advance, before the dairy year begins, what his quota will be for that year. The Commission gives an undertaking at that time that it will provide support in the marketplace for butterfat, skimmed milk powder and for cheese, not only in the amount specified, but for more.
The difficulty we are trying to deal with at the present time, is this: what are we to do about those who ignore the indications of what the demand is likely to be and ship in substantially more than their quotas provide? The hon. member knows that in one form or another, either through the holdback from the Dairy Commission or otherwise, it cost $35 million in the current year to dispose of surpluses, and the final figure may run even higher than that. I suggest that if we could reduce those surpluses and, hence, the cost of exporting them, by the amount of even one-third, the $10 million difference between the $125 million and the $115 million that we hear so much about would be fully taken care of as far as any subtraction from producers' returns is concerned. This is the problem to which, I suggest, we ought to be addressing ourselves.
I do not think we can ever predict with a precision some people might like, exactly what situation will develop in the marketplace during a year. However much people in the government, responsible for the treasury, or outside it, interested directly in the industry, might wish to do so, I do not believe it can be done. We do know that the trend in production is toward an increasing amount of skimmed milk powder and, now, butter will be in a surplus position. This is merchandise which is supported-the price for skimmed milk powder is 20 cents a pound. I would point out that skimmed milk powder has been selling on the international market at a price as low as six cents a pound, about one-third of what we pay our producers. We hope this situation will improve in the near future as a result of an international agreement among those countries which have built up great supplies of skimmed milk powder, and that
February 19, 1970	COMMONS
prices at the level I have mentioned will no longer be in effect, especially tor skimmed milk powder intended for human use.
The point I am making is this: there is no reasonable market for these dairy products internationally. In fact, there is no market in the world at all at a price anywhere near what the dairy farmers of Canada will accept for their products. Inside our own Canadian market we can, of course, effectively control prices and competition from dumping by sources outside Canada. Consequently, returns are at a level which, though they may not be the highest in the world, are certainly not the least. Indeed, they are very close to being the highest as far as returns from the Canadian people for dairy products are concerned if one takes into account the level at the support price plus the $100 million or so which is put into the industry annually by the taxpayers of Canada.
I do not have time today to go into all of these matters but I should like to refer directly to the wording of the motion put forward by the hon. member. He asks the House to condemn government policy in connection with the dairy industry-
For having stated its dairy policy for 1969-70 at the very last moment, namely on March 31, 1969, and not having taken into account recommendations from producers concerned.
Well, it is a fact that the dairy policy was announced on March 31, the last day of the support year. The practice of announcing the dairy support program only shortly before the start of a new dairy year is one which has been followed each year and for a very good reason-it was a particularly good reason last year. Hon. gentlemen are aware that the dairy support program embraces not only the direct subsidy but also the purchase policy in respect of the three basic commodities-butter, cheese and skimmed milk powder. Last year there was a very significant change in the level of production which became apparent to us and to the Dairy Commission after the first of the year, after January 1, 1969. Previous levels up to September, 1968, would indicate we needed a small amount of butter imported into Canada to balance the requirement of our market, bearing in mind that there is always skimmed milk powder going along with the butter. If there is to be only a reasonable surplus of skimmed milk powder then there will, of course, have to be a slight shortage of butterfat in the marketplace. So it was thought in September, 1968, that we
DEBATES	3843
Government Dairy Policy might need a few pounds of butterfat to keep the market supplied for the balance of the year.
It turned out-and this did not become apparent until after January, 1969,-that there had been a significant increase in the total production of milk, and, in particular, of butter, along with the skimmed milk powder which accompanies its production. This increase took place in the last two months of 1968 and it was accentuated in the early months of 1969. We were obliged to take this into account because we are required, as responsible members of the government, to budget on the basis of the levels for which provision had been made.
The other suggestion in the motion that the government failed to take into account recommendations from the producers concerned is not correct. We agree that requests from the producers for substantial increases in federal expenditure associated with increased levels of support were not acceded to. I do not have to repeat the arguments I put forward earlier today with respect to this subject. But before decisions were made, extensive consultation took place with producer organizations as a result of which many recommendations by the producers associated with minimum and maximum eligibility figures, methods of handling quota applications and other items of quota administration became part of the 1969 policy.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
In addition to that, the policy included minimum quality standards in accordance with producer recommendations. Broad suggestions were made by the producers which were also implemented, including a step in the direction of agricultural adjustment and a joint study of production management.
I come now to the second part of the motion, which reads:
For having contributed to reducing the dairy producers' income by cutting down the subsidies and increasing the export tax;
For 1969, the support level was not lowered. While the total assistance was increased, this increase was based on the need for additional funds to cover expanded production. This relates directly to the increased cost of exporting the surplus.
The third paragraph of the motion reads as follows:
For having listed in the 1970-71 estimates a reduction in the dairy industry subsidies, which will further reduce the dairy producers' income.
February 19, 1970

Government Dairy Policy
I mentioned the joint study with the producers of production management programs. Many hon. members are well aware that the dairy farmers of Canada, through the national dairy organization, have suggested a program of market quotas which will serve both as an agent to production and management and also better to allocate to those responsible for surplus production the cost of moving surpluses into offshore markets.
I cannot stress too strongly that the implementation of such a program, which I suggest lies largely outside the jurisdiction of this government, will do more to assist the income of producers who are tailoring their production to domestic requirements. Current estimates indicate that were the need for export assistance to be removed, producers would be able to receive anywhere from 25 to 35 cents per hundredweight more for quota milk than is presently the case.
Before I conclude my remarks, I should like to congratulate the Standing Committee on Agriculture for the consideration it has given the matter and on the report that it has made to the House. I think that regardless of what happens later with the report, or indeed the amendment before the House, this has been a very useful exercise in ascertaining the views of a large number of people across the country. The Department of Agriculture and the Canadian Dairy Commission have had people in attendance at, I believe, every one of the meetings which were open to them. This has enabled them to ascertain dairy farmers' views in advance of our setting out our policy for 1970-71.
This was partly the reason that in November last I announced that we needed advice; that we wished to receive the advice from those knowledgeable in the country about this matter in order to help us formulate a plan to bring this surplus production within reasonable range of the market. As I have said, as far as I am concerned this exercise has been helpful.
It might also be of assistance at this point briefly to review the situation which led to the reference that was made to this committee. I suggest that the history of federal price support has been a rather long one. For example, from 1948 to 1958 this federal assistance took the form entirely of supporting the market price of the three major dairy products, namely butter, cheese and skim milk powder. The market price of these products, as established under the price supports, determined the price which the processors paid the producers for manufacturing milk and cream.

Subsidies to producers started in 1959, but from then until 1966 were designed only to compensate for a withdrawal of, or reduction in product support prices. There was a minor supplementary subsidy payment in 1965, but the payment of producer subsidies in their present form, in addition to and supplementary to the support of product prices, may be considered to have started in 1966.
Whether or not there is complete agreement that the total returns to producers from the marketplace and from subsidies are adequate, it seems clear that some steps ought to be taken to avoid a risk which always accompanies the assurance of a reasonably satisfactory price. The risk is that it encourages production that is beyond the ability of the market to absorb.
The first step to this end was taken in 1966, when a deduction or holdback was made from the subsidy payments to finance the loss involved in exporting products surplus to Canadian requirements. This established the principle that the cost of disposing of such surpluses was a charge against the industry.
The next step was taken in 1967, when a limit was placed on the amount of manufacturing milk and cream on which subsidy would be paid. This quantity was placed at the approximate requirements of the total Canadian market for dairy products on a butterfat basis. This total amount was, in turn, divided among producers by individual subsidy eligibility quotas on the basis of the quantity which each had delivered in previous years. This established the principle that any milk or cream which producers shipped in excess of their quotas would not be eligible for subsidy.
Then in 1967 and 1968, there was another holdback on this excess milk at the same rate as on quota milk, and the amount was deducted from the subsidy payments. I should also point out that in 1969 the rate of holdback on over-quota deliveries was placed at a level that was substantially higher than, indeed double, that of the holdback on inquota deliveries.
Unfortunately, these measures have not prevented an increase in the amount of product that is surplus to Canadian requirements. The principal surplus has been in skim milk powder. In 1966 Canadian production whs about 100 million pounds greater than Canadian consumption. Last year the surplus was over 200 million pounds. I am talking about 200 million pounds in excess of the
February 19, 1970	COMMONS
requirements of the Canadian market, which is about 165 million to 170 million pounds.
The cost of disposing of this in export markets, plus the export subsidy required to maintain our traditional market for cheddar cheese in the United Kingdom, must be recovered from the funds provided for subsidies. The cost is, therefore, a direct charge against producer returns. This is assuming that we will use all of the funds that are allocated to the dairy support program; in fact, experience over past years has been that we do, and then some. As I say, the cost is therefore a direct charge against these returns.
At the present time this expense, as exlpained to the committee, is using up about one-third of total subsidy funds. That is to say, of the $125 million, about one-third of the total amount coming out of the treasury is used to dispose of surpluses.
There is at present a serious world surplus of dairy products, and export prices are seriously depressed as a consequence. One encouraging recent development is that as a result of negotiations at Geneva under GATT, agreement has been reached among the major exporting countries for a minimum export price on skim milk powder for human consumption. We hope that this is successful in raising that price, at least to some degree, and of course to the degree that it is successful it will reduce the export losses on this commodity to the Canadian Dairy Commission and subsequently to the Canadian dairy producer.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
The export situation with butter, however, is even more serious than with skim milk powder. There was a sale reported recently from Europe to South America at about ten cents per pound. The Canadian price for but-terfat, as is well known, is supported at 65 cents per pound.
Until recently excess butterfat has not been of concern in Canada because it was just about in balance until the end of 1968. In 1969 the Canadian consumption of butter was 14 million pounds more than the production. Last year, however, production exceeded consumption by 28 million pounds. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Dairy Commission now owns 30 million pounds more butter than it did a year ago, and this is close to 10 per cent of the annual Canadian production.
DEBATES	3845
Government Dairy Policy
As a result we are now faced with a butter surplus which could become quite serious if present production and consumption trends continue. It is clear, therefore, that we must devise and apply policies that will reduce, if not eliminate, these surpluses and bring a better balance between the production of dairy products and the effective demand for them at Canadian support prices, or at some price that is reasonable to the dairy farmers of Canada.
I see I am nearly running out of time, Mr. Speaker, so I will not go into all the rest of the details. But I want to say this in conclusion. There is no one more keenly interested in maximizing or increasing the returns to the dairy farmers in Canada than my party and the Department of Agriculture. In line with that, Mr. Speaker, we have to face the very real facts of life in Canada, in the dairy industry in Canada, and the dairy market in Canada. The facts are that we are running now at production levels that are about 10 per cent or 12 per cent above the consumption levels in Canada, and there is no market beyond our borders anywhere near the support price in Canada.
So, Mr. Speaker, if we can find ways, and I think we can in co-operation with the dairy industry, to set up first a system where we will bring into the market from the producers about what the Canadian market can absorb for all purposes, but of course particularly for human purposes, and then if there is any that comes in beyond that it should be the responsibility of those producers who are in fact shipping over their quotas to bear the major financial burden of disposing of that surplus production.
I think that in the ensuing year, and we have done a lot of calculating on this, if we could maintain the subsidy level at $1.25 per hundredweight, where it is today, we could maintain the holdback on the in-quota milk at 26 cents per hundredweight, where it is today, provided we were able to substantially increase the holdback on quota milk. But, Mr. Speaker, one of the problems involved in that is that because there is over-quota milk this does, in fact, finally arrive in our inventories in the form of skim milk powder and butter. At this point we do not have any subsidy payment at all, and therefore we do not have any withholding mechanism. Here I refer to the non-quota milk which is coming in, and I also refer in this context to over-quota shipments from the fluid milk dairy industry.
February 19, 1970

Government Dairy Policy
So again I appeal to hon. members on all sides of the House, and to the dairy industry, to help us complete designing a program that is not going to go on increasing the financial costs of getting rid of the surplus, but of finding a way of bringing butter production and consumption into balance at reasonable prices so that the dairy farmers of Canada can increase their net return.
