speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to take part in this debate. Needless to say I consider it of vital importance for the dairy industry and the dairy
February 19, 1970	COMMONS DEBATES	3847
farmers, not only of the province of Quebec but also of the whole country.
The minister (Mr. Olson) has told us of his department's achievements in the past few years. I am not one of those who believe that neither the minister nor his department have done anything in recent years, but I suggest that the question that should lie asked today is this: What has been done and is it enough?
Above all, I will not waste my time supporting the non-confidence motion introduced by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert), taking into account the problems now facing dairy farmers in Canada.
It is also clear that those days allocated to the opposition are remarkably useful. I noticed yesterday that due to the persistence of an opposition party, we were able to obtain an emergency debate on the difficulties affecting postal services in Montreal. Today, another opposition party enables us to discuss the problems of dairy farmers.
I know perfectly well, however, that the Quebec C.F.U. has been demanding an emergency debate for two or three months. This debate is necessary in order to allow the members of this House to discuss in detail the difficulties facing dairy farmers.
I would have wished, of course, that most government members from Quebec were more aware of the seriousness of the problem. I think that they are seven or eight. I wonder whether they recognize the importance of this debate as much as we have for a long time.
I will not provide any statistics since the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) gave some very valid ones, but I will hasten to ask hon. members to take today's debate very seriously, and I will also take this opportunity, as a member of the Standing Committee on Agriculture for a year and a half, to speak on the matter.
I had the privilege of travelling throughout Canada, of meeting various associations and of getting familiar with farming operations. On those trips, the committee was able to gather some information which allows us now to recognize the difficulties facing Canadian farmers, regardless of their activities.
That information enables us at the moment to make certain recommendations to the committee. We recognize the problems which affect the farmers generally.
After a year and a half as members of this committee, we might find with some frustration that we seldom make suggestions that are seriously studied and considered by the government.
Government Dairy Policy
I had an opportunity to mention this not long ago in committee. I shall surely not miss this opportunity to state the case in the House, since I have every reason to believe that there is a lack of consultation.
In fact, I shall take this opportunity to point out that some time ago, I put a question to the Minister of Agriculture. I asked him why the dairy policy was being announced only the day before its coming into effect. I was told that this was to allow organizations to submit briefs, that once these briefs had been examined and taken into consideration by the minister and his assistants, the policy could be devised according to needs.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Last week, when we discussed in committee the introduction of recommendations in the House, we found out that since the Blue Book or the Estimates had been tabled Wednesday, it was impossible for us to ask for supplementary grants. This shows irresponsibility and lack of consideration where the farmers are concerned.
With regard to the dairy industry, we are aware of all the economic difficulties both in Quebec and in Canada. Their very existence makes it impossible to turn a deaf ear to the recommendation now brought in by various associations in their briefs. I must also say how costly were the steps taken by the Canadian dairy associations in Quebec and elsewhere. Those agencies unanimously agreed on certain matters and arranged for initiating proceedings with the federal government to make themselves heard. I know very well that the committee, with only one dissenting voice, admitted that these briefs were excellent in essence and presentation.
After all these steps have been taken and all these expenses incurred, if the associations do not meet with a minimum of success, I wonder if the time is not ripe to tell the dairy producers to stop coming to Ottawa as under the circumstances their trips are utterly useless.
Lately a $10 million cut in subsidies was announced. I asked the Deputy Minister, who had been consulted, for some explanation and I received no answer. I asked what purpose was served by this committee. Indeed, when a cut of $10 million is announced, one begins to wonder. Nobody had ever heard of it. We were always led to believe that the committee served to formulate suggestions for the government's consideration.
February 19, 1970

Government Dairy Policy
Now, in view of these facts, I regret to have to say that the committee does not serve any purpose, as said earlier by an hon. member. In view of the position taken by this government, I am wondering how we will regain the confidence of the people. As a matter of fact, sometimes people seem to lose confidence in the government and Parliament.
At the present time, dairy producers are giving evidence of their good will by assuring the government of their collaboration as far as limiting their production is concerned. When the minister spoke of overproduction, he mentioned that this was the major problem facing the dairy industry. I realize that the minister certainly did not read the CFU submission, or he would not have spoken of overproduction as a problem it is hard to cope with. It might be useful if I in turn mentioned some of the recommendaitons of the report. Thus they will be on record in Hansard and the minister might keep them in mind. The Quebec dairy producers offered their co-operation, expressed their interest and made the following recommendations, which I quote:
-in agreement with other Canadian organizations and particularly the Canadian Dairy Producers, the dairy producers of Quebec accept for the next dairy year a quota system for marketing all industrial milk (surplus fluid milk, quota industrial milk, above quota industrial milk and non-quota industrial milk) under which the production of each farmer over and above the 1969-70 level would be marketed at the international export market price, whatever its level.
To facilitate the introduction of this system, a certain flexibility in its application would surely be considered.
Another recommendation is to the effect that the producers:
Eventually accept a reduction in production, according to terms and conditions to be determined, but below the 1969-70 level-
Finally, they agree to fully co-operate in an adjustment of production to market requirements in the establishment of programs designed to expand markets for milk and milk products, especially sales promotion programs-
Those are suggestions which have been mentioned from time to time but to which the government has turned a deaf ear.
I continue the quotation:
-of dairy products, food assistance programs for low income groups, school children-

meaning free milk in Canadian schools-
-various social institutions and developing countries as well as programs to promote a greater use of dry skimmed milk in animal feed.

They agree to co-operate in adjustment measures to help some categories of farmers to abandon farming in measures taken by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion as well as in all other agricultural policies promoting the diversification of agriculture.
What has been done to prepare those who would like to leave their farms? Was serious consideration given to early retirement or to the granting of subsidies for each cow sold, in order to transform the producer's activities? I wonder whether those proposals were seriously considered by the government.
Today, we are discussing a motion in which the government is held responsible for known hardships.
Those difficulties are no doubt due to the economic situation. I wonder how one can believe that the proposal to reduce the Canadian Dairy Commission's budget by $10 million, a large amount for dairy farmers, can be acceptable.
In view of the increased costs of production and services, it would have been better to recommend an increase of 5 per cent, which would have given an additional sum ranging from $20 to $22 million.
We are beginning to think that it is impossible to suggest an increase through a brief, because the estimates have already been tabled.
I know that dairy farmers and the people are tempted to laugh when they are told not to advocate or suggest the adoption of such measures because the estimates have been tabled.
Does that mean that the estimates have been tabled too soon? Is it honest on the part of the minister to say that he is waiting for the presentation of these briefs-once again, we all agree that they are excellent-to implement his policy, when immediately after he shifts the onus onto another department, saying that the estimates having been tabled it is inconceivable that subsidies should be increased this year.
However, a reduction was ordered. I think that is unacceptable for all members who believe that there are problems right now in agriculture. Given the economic situation, it is unthinkable that these subsidies should be cut down. On the contrary, they should be increased.
The government which would not pay attention to the recommendations we are making today would be implementing an inhuman policy as regards milk producers and all those directly affected.
It is clear that some producers are worried today. Many of them in Quebec and else-
February 19, 1970	COMMONS
where in Canada are tormented at present. The fact that many milk producers are here today in the galleries shows clearly how seriously they consider the real problems which now exist.
The drastic decisions taken recently in the House and the austerity program to fight inflation have resulted in inhuman measures.
It makes me laugh when they talk about austerity or say that the most important problem at the present time is inflation. It is a known fact that the most important problem is unemployment. In view of the very great number of unemployed it is inconceivable to force farmers on the labour market, since there are no jobs available.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
It is obvious that if we endeavoured to create more employment, we could see the small producers who are experiencing difficulties turn by themselves towards the labour market, and we would not have to resort to a policy of dissuasion. In fact, the present $10 million cut, as well as the prospect of an eventual elimination of subsidies give us the feeling that the government wants to apply a policy of dissuasion.
Is there anything more inhuman on the part of the government than to lack the courage, to offer clear-cut solutions in order to retrain the farmers who have to abandon the land to work in some other fields.
We must face that problem today. I suppose most of the hon. members will be sufficiently interested in that industry to stand up for it as it is really in need. I remember that hardly 18 or 20 months ago, the government had promised the farmers an adequate income supplement, which was to provide stability again in their case and enable them to keep their farm.
There is not a single member who did not see fit to make such promises and today we do not have the courage to say clearly that there is no future for a certain group of producers. The policy that is applied is rather one of discouragement which is most unsound and inhuman.
May I also be allowed to say that most government members, 56 or whom come from Quebec, promised the dairy producers that they would find the answers to their problems. In spite of these commitments, they very seldom have been seen to take a positive stand.
Last night, on the emergency debate, the opposition are the ones who asked that such a stand be taken. Today, it is once again the 21701-33J
DEBATES	3849
Government Dairy Policy members of the opposition who allow the dairy producers to be heard. I wonder exactly how many government members will take part in this debate and will urge the minister to grant once more to the dairy producers the subsidy of $10 million or more which represents the 5 per cent which is absolutely necessary to maintain a minimum standard of living.
These things have to be told and as members of this house we must show some objectivity. As for me, I am pleased to support the motion under consideration although it was moved by a member outside of my party because I think that objectivity must prevail over politics, as I have mentioned on different occasions. The minister had the opportunity earlier to say that he had reconsidered the matter and restored the $10 million subsidy, but who can tell what game the minister is playing now.
The cancellation of the $10 million dairy industry subsidy, as announced a few weeks ago, will force the Quebec Dairy Producers Association as well as all producers throughout Canada to work that much more to recover the amount which should never have been cancelled. Nor will they have the time to ask for the additional help required.
If tomorrow morning the Minister of Agriculture were to announce that he is willing to reconsider his decision and to restore that $10 million subsidy, all would be well. It behooves the members to recommend to the government that it restore that $10 million subsidy the milk producers absolutely need.
As strange as it may seem when the Minister of Agriculture announced, some time ago, that he was thinking, because of the austerity program, of reducing by $10 million the budget of the Canadian Dairy Commission, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) announced, while in Quebec, that he expected a budget surplus of $500 million.
I say the dairy producers are justified in being concerned and in wondering whether the government is really serious when it speaks of bringing back stability to agriculture. On the one hand, it states that it expects a $500 million surplus and on the other hand it admits to being forced to reduce by $10 million the budget of the Canadian Dairy Commission because austerity so dictates.
One wishes to establish a just society. I wonder for whom this society will be just when we know that agriculture in Quebec represents an important part of our economy.
February 19, 1970

Government Dairy Policy We cannot remain silent in front of these cuts and of this policy. It is not the first time that the present government does something prejudicial to the interests of the farmers.
One is now dead against an industry which is the tobacco industry. I find rather strange that the ministers interested in this industry have not talked to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) who is only hurting this industry, one of the few, in Canada, that need no subsidy from the government to remain active.
And I have not heard a single word from the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cote), who gets from this industry $600 million in taxes. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Maeka-sey), who should have enough unemployed people to deal with, as well as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) have not made any comment. We would like to assure them, once for all, that they will be able to continue their operations with enough cattle to provide their family with a better future.
It is not the first time, Mr. Speaker, that these farmers are coming to Ottawa. Today, they came back in limited numbers. A few years ago, they were here in greater numbers, staging marches on Ottawa. Results are slow to materialize and I understand then-impatience and concern.
I do hope this debate will bring about something practical, and that the present government will do something to alleviate the concern of these dairy producers.
I was, of course, expecting the Minister of Agriculture to remain in the House for this debate, hoping he would take the trouble to listen to the suggestions brought forth by hon. members.
I am sure that some time, later on, some government members will make suggestions to the minister on the ground of objectivity and public interest. I remember the hearings of the committee where most hon. members supported the briefs which were submitted.
The ministers from Quebec or from the other provinces, should enter this debate and compel the government to take action to help so as to stabilize our dairy industry and ensure our dairy producers of the full support of their members.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I v/elcome the opportunity to speak in this debate and appreciate the motion made by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert). However, I have been interested in the fact that there was not a cabinet minister in the House for the last half hour. I wonder if it is because of a lack of interest in agriculture or is it because the debate has been in French. I hope that neither is the case.
Late last fall, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) referred this matter of the austerity program to the agriculture
February 19, 1970

committee with instructions that they were to consider ways of disposing of the $10 million agricultural subsidy in a manner that would least upset the agricultural sector, namely, the dairy industry. We have had a number of meetings since that time, Mr. Speaker, and a number of representations from the dairy industry of Canada, including the National Dairy Farmers of Canada and the CCC, both organizations representing a large number of the fluid and industrial milk producers of this nation. The results of the meetings were that, not only should we reinstate the $10 million into the subsidy program but we should in fact add to it in a number of ways.
I think the fact that this matter has been raised very eloquently by the hon. member for Bellechasse today and the support it has received here and in committee, is an indication that the situation is very much as outlined. I get letters from the industrial milk producers in my area. My riding lies close to the Quebec boundary for 100 or 150 miles in Northern Ontario, so the problem there is not much different from that facing some of the people sitting in the gallery today who come from that province. They were plagued last year with too much rain at harvest time and then a very difficult spring. As a result they had poor hay and, in many cases, very little grain. While it may have been possible to operate this way a few years ago the fact is that, like all farmers, they have borrowed to the hilt in order to be able to produce for the fluid and industrial milk markets. They have bought additional cattle and have increased the capacity of their barns. In many cases, they have had to buy additional land and have put in bulk coolers as well as other equipment necessary for dairy production. Now, they are in the position of producing considerably more milk than the market can absorb.
In my area the Ontario government controls both fluid milk production and industrial milk production. When the milk comes from the cow it is owned by the Ontario government who disposes of it to the dairies or any other source that they can find. Milk, therefore, becomes the commodity of the government as soon as it goes into the bulk cooler. The surprising thing is that we in the little clay belt of Northern Ontario are producing fluid milk for the area and sending the surplus into Quebec, where it becomes milk powder in the Montreal market. We, therefore, are considerably involved with the problems developing in the province of Quebec. There must be some relationship between the two provinces.
Government Dairy Policy
A few years ago, about 1963, I read some of the literature put out by the Liberal party at election time. I think it was sent to me inadvertently because it was addressed to the Liberal candidate at that time. It indicated that they were going to get rid of small farmers in Canada. A number of programs were announced which would achieve that end. I congratulate the Liberal party for having succeeded in getting rid of most of our small farmers.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Part of the problem in western Canada, and other parts of the country, is that it no longer seems possible for a farmer to enter the dairy business. A farmer with a little money to spare can no longer afford to buy three or four extra cows and become a dairy producer. There is no room for him in the Ontario dairy industry either as a producer of fluid or industrial milk unless, in addition to buying his cows and farm, he can buy a quota. It has been said that many farmers in parts of western Canada, northern Quebec and northern Ontario ought not to produce milk. Perhaps that is true. We must remember that the foundations of this country rest on our rural economy. Twenty or thirty years ago our economy was more rural oriented than today. A large number of constituencies represented in this House are rural constituencies and the subject of agriculture gives rise to as many debates as at least five other subjects put together.
We debate agriculture because agriculture is important to us. A dairy farmer cannot enter dairy production with four or five cows these days because his facilities may not meet minimum requirements. At one time a farmer perhaps had several milk cows and two or three calves. He may have been feeding a brood sow and several pigs; his wife may have kept 20 or 30 chickens. In those days, the money coming in from cream production subsidized the farm income. That situation is now changed. We find that very little cream is being produced in my area. One of our creameries is in very serious straits and another that used to ship carloads of butter in winter and summer is working on a part-time basis. The same is true of a third outlet in my area which is also having difficulty. I think the people involved in these operations will agree that the government ought to support cream production.
In my hand I have a letter that I received from farmers in the township of Hudson. It
February 19, 1970

Government Dairy Policy says that farmers in Hudson township who have been raising veal calves are, "not going to be able to get the calves" because the dairymen will be forced to raise their own calves for veal in order to keep milk production down. On the other hand, as the letter says, the veal calf man is not going to be able to get calves. This will necessitate this farmer milking cows, thus placing more butterfat on the market. More than likely, this farmer will be out of business because of lack of income. The letter goes on to say that, "normally, bull calves in this area at this time of the year"- the area referred to being my area of northern Ontario-"sold for $15.00 to $20.00. Now, these same calves are selling for $40.00 to $50.00, if available at all."
It is clear that if you play around with the farming sector of the economy you will create difficulties. It behooves us to change our system and put right the things wrong with it. I was interested in hearing a government spokesman say that we can not sell more wheat. As a matter of fact, there is no government agency that will buy directly any farm commodity. The government really is not in the business, except in a very limited way, of buying or selling anything on behalf of the Canadian population.
It might be a good idea if an agency of government could enable farmers to exchange farm produce for tractors. We are having great difficulty obtaining tractors at reasonable prices. A man came to my brother's place the other day and said he could get him a David Brown tractor for $4,000 less than he would have to pay downtown. If bodies like the Ontario Federation of Agriculture could make sure that our farmers could buy tractors in Ontario at the price, the saving to the farmer on his farm machinery costs would be so great that some parts of farm production would not have to be subsidized. Farmers in this country are always going to be in trouble because of their ability to overproduce.
Since I have been here I have watched us throw away millions of pounds of butter which was reduced to butter oil. We could not get rid of the butter. The factory in British Columbia storing it was burned; I suppose somebody collected the insurance. We have always been able to produce surpluses, because every time the farmer is told to produce more of any commodity he produces so much that you have a surplus. The problem is that we have never tried very hard to sell our surpluses. We asked people from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce


appearing before the Committee on Agriculture whether the government sells farm produce, and we were informed that it does not. Our farmers are told, "If you go to such and such a place you will find a buyer for your produce at such and such a price." The point is that the government does not sell this produce on behalf of an important segment of the Canadian public.
Some may say that it is foolish for a premier of a province to go outside his province with a boat load of wheat and come back with a generator for a hydro plant. I am not sure that is good business; on the other hand, I am not sure that is wrong, because at least the wheat is disposed of and a generator is acquired at a reasonable price. We are one of the few countries in the world that has no government buying and selling agency to deal with farm produce, and I think it is about time we investigated this aspect.
I now wish to talk about the matter of cutting $10 million from the year's dairy allotment. Mir. Speaker, not one member of the Standing Committee on Agriculture, I am sure, would have been opposed to increasing the allotment by the $10 million demanded by the Ontario Marketing Board and the dairy farmers of Canada. As I say, not one committee member would have opposed increasing the allotment over that of last year by $10 million. When the matter came before the committee, we were told by legal advisers that the suggestion was in order. But what did the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) do? He came in and, on raising a technical point, argued that the suggestion was not in order and the allotment was therefore cut by $10 million.

The day will come when Canadian farmers will not be able to produce all the food the world needs. I remember a few years ago how much trouble we had in my area getting a pulp and paper mill to locate there. It seemed that no one was interested in setting up a pulp and paper mill because there was a world surplus of pulp and paper. Today a number of pulp and paper mills are being built in Canada. We are going to find that we are five or ten years late in our maximum production of paper to meet the world demand.
February 19, 1970	COMMONS
One of these days we are going to find we are short in every commodity we produce in the agricultural sector. I do not think anyone in his right mind would say there is too much wheat, protein, butter or skim milk powder in the world. The difficulty is we have not found out how to dispose of that and provide a reasonable return for the farmer. This government talks about reducing everything to curb inflation. They have already reduced the farmer to a very low level in terms of any surplus. This has been deflationary. In most cases, the farmer has alreader been paying a 52 cent hold-back in the fluid milk market and a 26 cent hold-back on industrial milk. It is not the government that is paying this, it is the farmer. The farmer makes these payments to dispose of a surplus which he did not create directly.
I suggest this government would be well advised to restore the $10 million. For the first time, this government has had an offer from most of the farm organizations in the dairy industry to do something about overproduction. This is a problem that has always been with us and will continue in the future. It will have to be met by the farmers. In return for that, the government will have to guarantee them a parity price which should be at least the cost of production plus their wages.
I agree with the hon. member for Belle-chasse (Mr. Lambert) that the flat wage on the farm is probably 88 cents an hour or approximately at that level. The hired men of this country are only receiving $200 or $300 a month plus some fringe benefits. This means most farmers find that the hired man's wages represents the total profit on the business. I talked to some very efficient farmers, one of whom was my brother. I think he is probably as efficient as any farmer in my part of the country. He knows what is going on because he belongs to all the organizations. We have been on ROP for years. We have been operating a thoroughbred dairy herd for a number of years. My brother has some college education. He told me that the amount of money he had left out of a total income on his farm operation, which I consider is worth probably $150,000, amounted to less than $3,000. If he has to pay another hired man that $150,000 farm operation will be a non-operable operation.
For years most farmers have operated on depreciation. I can remember during the war when my father was very active in farm organizations. He talked about the sacrifice
DEBATES	3853
Government Dairy Policy the farmers were making on behalf of the war effort and the fact that they were making this contribution for patriotic reasons. That sort of patriotic contribution is still being made at the present time. The government is spending $50 million to aid bilingualism. They could probably spend another $50 million to provide a viable farm operation across this nation. The farmers will do all they can to help. The farm organizations have agreed they will provide, police and help operate a quota system for all milk. To the best of my knowledge, milk is being pooled in Ontario. This is also true in British Columbia. I understand that step is being considered in the province of Quebec. Milk will soon all be in one bucket, controlled by one agency for sales purposes.
The producers have said they will co-operate. They will set some limits. It is up to the government to decide whether they will pay a price which would enable these dairy farmers to continue their operation. If the aim of this government is to get rid of all these farmers here in the gallery, most of whom I imagine are small farmers, and have the farms operated by Steinberg's or the feed mills, then there will be vertical integration of these farm operations. All the government needs to do is cut back on dairy support as well as the support provided to some other segments of agriculture today, and we will have vertical integration.
The people of Canada will have to pay higher prices. Milk will cost 50 cents a quart. The price of butter and other agricultural products will increase. The Canadian people will then find out how stupid they have been to support the economies of this government. They are false economies which are not doing anything for the consumer or the agricultural segment of our nation.

This practice is widespread in the province of Quebec because the producers were told to improve their production and to produce more. Now that they have become competent, we want to discourage them by punishing them and depriving them of $10 million in subsidies.
Far from letting farmers keep up with the increasing cost of living, we want them to support the full load of a reduction in subsidies, something which spells disaster and suicide for farmers. This compensated discount existed during wartime. The hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) demanded a while ago that money be made available to individuals and that the compensated discount be established to decrease the consumption cost.
When consumers are unable to pay the producers for their production, the government, through the Bank of Canada, should grant a compensated discount that would make it possible to purchase Canada's total production. The latter would increase both in quantity and in quality and, as a result, we would be able to adopt the same measures as in the United States where a survey carried out in the schools has shown that, when the price of the half-pint of milk was reduced from 10 cents to 3 cents, consumption increased by 180 per cent. In primary schools, sales of milk at 3 cents per half-pint have increased by 208 per cent.
If, through the Bank of Canada, it was decided to grant a compensated discount to consumers who cannot afford milk at current

prices, this would be a good thing. That is the responsibility of the government. Assuming that the government wishes to establish a just society as it claims, it should, instead of lending $1 million to Korea without interest, grant this loan to Quebec farmers.
If the government can afford to spend $7,500,000 for Information Canada, it must also spend money to promote agriculture, thus giving Canada a sound balance which is sorely needed. Our farmers have been too long neglected.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to conclude because time is running out. I would like to speak about the recommendations made by the Catholic Farmers' Union. It is said that the Canadian Dairy Commission's budget should not be reduced for 1970-71, so that it will not end up with a deficit. The $10 million reduction announced by the Minister of Agriculture should be cancelled.
I am making this request on behalf of the 25,000 people who signed the petition tabled yesterday, as well as of the members of the C.F.U.
Besides, the budget of the Canadian Dairy Commission should be increased. Considering the quota they have registered with the Canadian Dairy Commission, the producers would be guaranteed a total income for a hundredweight equal to that of the year 1969-70, and a sufficient surplus to compensate for the yearly 5 per cent cost increase for goods and services.
This request involves increasing the Canadian Dairy Commission's budget from $20 to $22 million, but it is essential to the survival of the farming people. Those who oppose it may, at the next election, meet the same fate as several hon. members in 1962, that is, defeat.

I am in sympathy with the suggestion of the hon. member for Belle-chasse (Mr. Lambert) whom I must commend for his work in the Standing Committee on Agriculture because more than 14 meetings were held in order to hear witnesses. I think that it was a very good thing for the committee on Agriculture to hear representations of all the farm associations. That suggestion was made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Cote).
The problems which we are up against with regard to milk are not unrelated to other farm problems. In agriculture, productivity, that is the net production per man, has increased since 1961 at the rate of 6.5 per cent per year. At the same time, productivity in all businesses increased at a much slower rate, that is 2.9 per cent per year.
Ten years ago, and in this regard I agree with the member for Bellechasse, one hour's wages allowed you to buy 7.2 quarts of milk whereas today you can buy ten. My time being very limited, I do not want to go into all the reasons for that. In any event, that is the situation our farmers are up against.
I should like, this evening, to analyse the situation and impress upon the officials of the department the importance of the dairy industry in the province of Quebec.
The dairy industry is basic to agriculture in Quebec. Indeed, over 50 per cent of the income of our farmers comes directly or indirectly from that industry. Almost 38 per cent of the total Canadian dairy production comes from the province of Quebec.
Our farmers are aware of present surpluses, for a look at the number of farmers registered with the Canadian Dairy Commission will reveal that in 1966-67 there were 53,342; in 1967-68, 49,660; in 1968-69, 45,116. From 1966 to 1969, 8,226 producers in Quebec were denied the right to subsidies.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
I think our farmers are aware of that surplus. The federal subsidy on industrial milk represents more than 20 per cent of the total income of the dairy industry in Quebec. I regard that situation as very important. In 1968-69, an amount of $43,000,366, representing 44 per cent of what was paid by the 21701-34J

Government Dairy Policy Canadian Dairy Commission, was precisely granted to the province of Quebec.
I wish to inform the House of such a situation for we are all aware that ideas of all kinds prevail in the province of Quebec. But I believe that this fact was never disclosed by the preachers we know.
So that goes to say that the farm economy in Quebec is more closely related to the dairy industry than in any other Canadian province. I deem it my duty, as a member from that province, to make the authorities aware of such conditions.
I am proud, of being a member of the Liberal party, for all the increases voted in favour of the Canadian Dairy Commission, in order to assist our dairy producers, were voted under Liberal governments.
I am also very much aware that, in the interest of dairy producers, the national dairy policy must have as a long term objective the development of an economic and productive dairy industry.
Considering the farm net income, compared with that of 1954, we find that the Quebec farmers are in a sorry plight. I mentioned at a meeting of the Standing Committee on Agriculture the following situation, namely that the 141 per cent increase in net income per farm, from 1954 to 1968, was accounted for by the producers of the three Prairie provinces.
In the Quebec province, from 1954 to 1968, the income increased by 14 per cent only while in Ontario it increased by 32 per cent. In one of the Maritime provinces the income went down 30 per cent whereas in British Columbia it went up 62 per cent.
All this because I do not want anybody to indulge in party politics, which seems to be the present trend. I do not want to by-pass the problem because I know how important the dairy industry is in Quebec.
We, Liberals, are aware of this. I would like to tell our detractors that from 1954 to 1960, the net income of the Quebec farmers decreased by $33 million From 1960 to 1966, the farmers of Quebec recorded an increase of $67 million of their net income and, from 1966 to 1968, under the present government, they experienced a decrease of about $8 million, but this is not the fault of the federal government.
I was reading yesterday, in a newspaper, a statement by the present Quebec Minister of Agriculture, to the effect that the only
February 19, 1970

Government Dairy Policy political party that has an agricultural doctrine is the Union Nationale. I think these figures can prove it.
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to continue to debate this matter, but I think these figures must be disclosed. I am very happy with the report that has been tabled in the House, although when this report was examined, I made some suggestions.
I think that where there is a problem of surpluses, there are always two methods of solving it.
The first one is to cut down production and the second, which to my mind is more logical, is to try and find markets and increase consumption at the domestic as well as the international level.
When we met with the officials of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, they explained their program and informed us of a more aggressive policy tending to the development of new products. We have to innovate in this field to increase consumption by all possible means as, according to present forecasts, we will face in 1980 a per capita decrease of 18 per cent in the consumption of dairy products of all kinds, which will be offset by an increase of 9 per cent due to population growth.
As regards present surpluses, the report of the Standing Committee on Agriculture is not very different from the brief presented by the Catholic Farmers Union. In fact, it can be seen on page 3 of this brief, and I quote:
Direct subsidies paid to producers have therefore been as follows:
1967- 68	$ 98.3 million
1968- 69	101.0 million
1969- 70	91.0 million
In 1970-71 there will be a reduction due to surpluses, but I repeat we will have to make an effort to use these surpluses and I believe that after having enforced an aggressive policy in the search for new markets and in trying to increase domestic consumption, we should also study the possibility of transforming this excess powdered milk into veal. I feel that this new possibility could ensure an additional income to the farmer.
I well remember that in 1962, when milk base products were introduced for calf feeding, the average price of veal was perhaps around $15, $20 or $25 cwt., but it is now, as you know, 45 to 48 cents a pound.
I would suggest that surplus milk waiting in warehouses be used to feed calves being raised for consumption.
[Mr. Roy (Laval) .1
Mr. Speaker, I would not like to take up another hon. member's time and I believe several of them want to express their opinion but we are facing a situation which it is hard to cope with. Actually, we are aware of the problem, we will give serious consideration to all possible solutions. I believe that the two problems now facing agriculture are the surpluses of wheat and milk.
I would like to see the government give the same attention to those two problems which are now curbing the development of our agriculture.
In closing, I congratulate the members of the CFU who are with us today. Their presence gave us much encouragement. It also proves the interest of farmers in the situation of the dairy industry. Such action is certainly commendable. I strongly urge the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) and all cabinet members to give consideration to the importance of the dairy industry and to use the $10 million which are not now in the Canadian Dairy Commission credits for other purposes in order to improve the present situation of Canadian agriculture.
I do not believe our farmers like to have welfare problems settled at their expense. Our farmers are too proud of their profession to be satisfied with promises alone. They are aware of the situation and I think there is certainly a way to find a solution to this problem by every possibility of improving technical methods.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak on the motion now under study, on behalf of the 900 farmers in my riding who signed the petition asking for this debate on Canada's dairy industry.
I sincerely believe that such a debate was urgently needed. Indeed, the dairy industry of the industrial sector enables more than 130,000 families-including 45,000 in the province of Quebec-to obtain a major part of their income.
It is undeniable that the dairy policy of the Canadian government has a very direct influence on the income of farmers in the riding of Beauce and in the rest of the province of Quebec.
The place occupied by the milk industry in Canada's farm economy does not necessarily correspond to the wishes of the farmers themselves, but it is the result of a trend initiated and promoted by the federal government.
The dairy policy as a whole must he aimed at providing a fair income for the efficient producer. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. February 19, 1970

Olson) said so himself at the annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Milk Producers held in Quebec City in January 1969, when he defined the role of the Canadian Dairy Commission and the long-term objective of the Canadian government in that respect.
Here is what he said, and I quote:
The extent of this intervention was confirmed in 1966 by the adoption of the Canadian Dairy Commission Act, with a view to providing fair returns to producers whose system is efficient, and adequate supplies of dairy products for the Canadian consumers.
Such is the long-term objective which the Canadian government is aiming at.
The main long-term objective of the government as regards the dairy industry is the stabilization of milk prices in order to guarantee a fair income to the producer. Disregarding this objective or taking a backward step would very likely force a great many producers into bankruptcy or simply, although indirectly, force them to leave the farm sector.
In view of the present attitude of the federal government, we may wonder as to whether this is not the purpase of the government.
The changes made in April 1969 to the dairy policy by the federal government and the Canadian Dairy Commission in particular, and those they intend to bring in, that is a reduction of $10 million in subsidies, as well as the development of the dairy industry during these last years are so many factors which have contributed during the last two or three years to lower appreciably the net income of Canadian and Quebec farmers in particular. Such a decrease in income occurs at a time when the cost of goods and services to farmers as well as the cost of living on the farms increase day by day.
The farmer, like any other worker, has to put up with inflation whose effects are painfully felt. Many farmers have had to give up production and if the government implements the policy envisaged many more will give up.
Inflation decreases the real income of superannuated people and others who have fixed incomes and makes it difficult to carry out the essential objective of guaranteed minimum incomes. Inflation can also slow down development, an essential objective.
Farmers made huge contributions to reaching that objective. The farm price index has increased only by 19 per cent from 1949 to 1967, while the retail price index and the
Government Dairy Policy wholesale price index increased respectively by 49 per cent and 32 per cent respectively during the same period.
Farmers were able to limit the increase of farm product prices to such a low percentage while other segments of the economy increased considerably more, thanks to the major investments they have made during the last two decades, to the improvement of their livestock and facilities. Those are so many factors which have contributed to the improvement of the quality of their production and to a higher efficiency.
Whether it be in the western or eastern provinces, agriculture in general is meeting serious difficulties and we cannot afford to let it stagnate.
Besides, the dairy industry is not the only industry subsidized by the government. Others such as collieries, transportation companies, gold mines, receive major subsidies. Bearing in mind the number of people employed by these industries, the subsidies granted them are as high as those granted the dairy industry. Moreover, is not the tariff protection enjoyed by some industries some kind of disguised subsidies?
Let us suppose that an important number of dairy producers gave up production to undertake other farming activities, or to go on an early pension owing to anticipated pension plans, it would nevertheless be necessary to create jobs in other economic sectors. However, this would cost about $30,000 per job and at times more, without taking into consideration investments required for housing, social and other services.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
The lack of investment capital is presently deplored, and the government is forever announcing new programs, apart from creating new jobs. There are comparative successes here and there, but the objectives decided upon are far from being reached.
As for the use of manpower in other sectors of the economy, it does not appear likely, even if those people were encouraged to take advantage of the intensive retraining programs. This appears even less likely in eastern Canada where the unemployment rate is high.
In any event, those who would be the first to suffer from this disruption are the producers over 45 years of age. It would be difficult for them to acquire new professional skills and to adapt to an urban environment. At any rate, according to the report of the planning commission, which deals with the
3864	COMMONS DEBATES	February 19, 1970
Government Dairy Policy problem of low-yield farms, during the next decade it will be extremely difficult to create in the other sectors of the economy enough jobs to take care of the normal flow of people from rural areas.
In the constituency of Beauce it will be very difficult, I think, for displaced persons to get immediate employment in the shoe, textile, manufacturing or lumbering industries because during these last months such industries had to lay off temporarily a great many workers and right now their production is lower than their capacity to produce due to lack of orders.
The textile industry is now slackening to a rather large extent. In St. George de Beauce, a plant whose staff normally comprises 275 employees had during these last weeks to lay off 50. It is expected that it will employ less than 200.
I understand it is difficult to dispose of the surplus dairy products on world markets which are already flooded with goods from Common Market countries.
Other industries, such as the footwear and textile industries, are also faced with problems resulting among other things from imports of products from Asian and European countries. Now I do not see the possibility of displacing farm labour, which will be affected by the intended changes, to the other areas of the economy to which I have just referred, because there already is a manpower surplus in those industries.
A few days ago, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) tabled the Estimates for 1970-71. I could see that large appropriations will be allocated to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, as well as to the Department of Manpower and Immigration, for the improvement of manpower. That increase totals close to $90 million.
I greatly appreciate the efforts that the government intends to make with respect to creating new jobs and retraining manpower, which in my opinion are projects of very great importance. However, I believe it just as important to concentrate our efforts in order to maintain existing jobs in agriculture as well as in industry, even if the government must allocate extra amounts to that end, as it should concerning the dairy industry, to allow the farmer to earn a decent income.
The approach of the producers to the matter is clear and definite. They want the price of milk to increase at the same rate as production and living costs. To reach that goal,

there is but one solution. The government should review its position and increase the grants paid to the Canadian dairy commission.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-INSUFFICIENCY OF GOVERNMENT MILK POLICY
speechtext: I find it difficult to take part in the debate tonight, Mr. Speaker, for several reasons. For many years I have been a member of the party which supports this government; I have been loyal for many years. But I must tell the House tonight that I simply do not agree with the policy of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) and the government in cutting $10 million off the subsidy to the Dairy Commission of Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-INSUFFICIENCY OF GOVERNMENT MILK POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-INSUFFICIENCY OF GOVERNMENT MILK POLICY
speechtext:
I am not sure whether that applause from my left is execution applause or not. In any event, those are my sentiments and I intend to stand by them in the time allotted to me tonight. I am not taking this course without having informed the members of my party; they appreciate the situation in which I am involved. I have let them know what my position is, both privately and in other places.
It is difficult to criticize the Minister of Agriculture, for several reasons. First, he is a very nice fellow and I am sure he was sincere when he said this afternoon that he was interested in giving the agricultural people of Canada a just deal. I have no doubt in the world that he was speaking the truth. I do not think we who are critical of the policy to be followed should put all the blame on the Minister of Agriculture. After all, he is only one member of the government, and when a substantial amount of money to the tune of $10 million is to be cut off I would say that the government as a whole should share the blame for it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-INSUFFICIENCY OF GOVERNMENT MILK POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-INSUFFICIENCY OF GOVERNMENT MILK POLICY
speechtext:
Since the minister is such a fine fellow and a real gentleman, I would say that when the first certificate is given for doing a good job in the anti-inflation drive it should be given to the Minister of Agriculture, because no sector of our economy has done more to fight inflation than agriculture-in particular, the dairy industry. In almost every area there have been cuts. The subsidy on hogs has been cut. That is good for the inflation battle. The subsidy on milk has been cut. That, too, is good for the inflation battle. The subsidy on freight rates for feed from western Canada has been cut. This
February 19, 1970

is not all. The price of many agriculture products is lower than it was several years ago. On this basis I would say the farmer and the Minister of Agriculture have done more to fight inflation than anyone in the land.
I want to make one thing clear. I am absolutely, completely and unalterably opposed to subsidy. As far as I am concerned, if we could do away with all subsidies in Canada I would be the first to stand and cheer. But as long as we provide subsidies for our coal mines, as long as auto manufacturers and the workers who make cars are subsidized through tariff protection and cars bought in Windsor or Oshawa cost $200 or $300 more than they do in Detroit, I think it is only right there should be subsidies for agriculture and in particular for those who work in the dairy industry. I see no justification whatsoever for lowering the subsidy at this time.
The agricultural industry, particularly the dairy industry, is at the low end of the economic totem pole. This is a situation which I do not wish to see continue. As a backbencher sent here to support the government, I believe we have an obligation to support it when it is right. But I say-I have also said it to my hon. friends in this chamber-that in addition to being sent here to support the government, we were sent to support the people back home.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-INSUFFICIENCY OF GOVERNMENT MILK POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-INSUFFICIENCY OF GOVERNMENT MILK POLICY
speechtext: Many of the people in my area are farmers and I do not have the slightest intention of letting them down, not one of them. Much was made this afternoon of the fact that there is considerable overproduction in the dairy industry. There is no question about this. The biggest surplus is in powdered milk, and I am told there is less powdered milk on hand today than was the case a year ago. It is true we have too much butter. I say to the Minister of Agriculture, to the government and to the salesmen who represent Canada all over the world: Get off your seats here in Ottawa. Get out into the world market and sell the stuff.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-INSUFFICIENCY OF GOVERNMENT MILK POLICY
speechtext:

speechtext:
Having had long experience in small business, I would say that the first loss is always the best loss. If you have to sell your product at a depressed price, do it today and not in five years' time. This will save you a lot of money in storage charges and we

Government Dairy Policy must remember that interest rates today are substantial. So long as the price is reasonable, sell your product.
After all, last year the minister told us that we were selling powdered milk at six or 6J cents a pound. Today we are selling powdered milk on the world market at 10 cents a pound. Last year the dairy subsidy was $125 million. This year, when the world market price has improved, the subsidy is being cut. As far as selling powdered milk is concerned, we have done a reasonably good job, though the price could of course always be improved.
Who subsidizes the sale of powdered milk in world markets? Does the government give any indication to some of our city friends who are possibly unfamiliar with the dairy business that the government is subsidizing powdered milk sales in world markets? Every member who comes from a rural riding will know that the dairy farmers of Canada subsidize their own overproduction and the amount of milk that is sold on world markets, and it is they who should get the credit for it. I should like someone to show me any other industry in Canada that subsidizes the sale of its own product as much as the dairy farmers of Canada subsidize theirs.
There is not a great deal more I wish to say; much has already been said. I want my constituents and the members of this House to know exactly where 1 stand on this question. As I said at the beginning, I am against subsidies. But something must be done for people in agriculture. Today there are half as many farmers in Canada as there were 20 years ago. We are slowly starving them into submission. As far as I and my vote are concerned, this is not the way agriculture should be treated.
Our farmers deserve the same treatment as that received by labour, which has had substantial increases in income over the years. Our corporations have also made larger profits. I do not deny them these for a moment; however, if every other sector of the economy has the right to move forward financially, so have those engaged in the dairy industry.
That is all I have to say, Mr. Speaker. Certainly I hope there is no member here tonight who does not know where I stand on the question of a dairy policy for Canada.

speechtext:
Although I come from Saskatchewan, let me say at once that I recognize that the dairy industry in Ontario and Quebec has problems and that the farmers need more money. Farmers everywhere are hemmed in by costs. As surely as the day will come when we will all die, the operations of dairy farmers will one by one be strangled by costs. In this respect they are no different from the dairy farmers of Saskatchewan.
I am not going to tell the House a story different from the one I tell the people of Saskatchewan. I want the people here tonight to know that we have every sympathy for them. We recognize they are not getting enough money for their products. I should also like them to know that according to the
tables I have presented to the House for consideration, out of a total of 30,000 people whose subsidies have been cut off, 10,000, or one third, came from Saskatchewan. These
10,000	people in my province have just as big a problem as those in our gallery tonight. I am not sure whether these 10,000 farmers all come from my constituency, but they do come from the province of Saskatchewan.

speechtext: They have been assisted by the Liberal government.

speechtext:
I hear my hon. friend from Toronto starting to interrupt, so let me pursue this matter further. All shippers who supplied less than 420 pounds of butterfat had
February 19, 1970

Government Dairy Policy their subsidies cut off. There are a lot of small farmers in Saskatchewan. According to the Minister without Portfolio from Saskatoon (Mr. Lang), these farmers are to be given two years holiday without pay. Is he going to give two years holiday without pay to the Quebec farmers? I ask this question because in that province last year there was a surplus of creamery butter amounting to 80 million pounds. Some may ask: Why is there alienation? Why are we worrying about what is happening in the west? Why are we talking about things in the way that we are? Well, Quebec spoke its piece and we are going to speak ours.
* (8:40 p.m.)
I am not one to be very shy in this House and I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the reason we are annoyed is that subsidies were taken away from 10,000 dairy producers in Saskatchewan and given to somebody else. This is what I am annoyed about. But that did not reduce the over-all subsidy and these people still deliver their cream. They do so because they need the dollars they get for it, irrespective of subsidy.
Do hon. members know what all those people who were cut off subsidy because they could not deliver 420 pounds of butterfat contributed to the national output in the last two years? Saskatchewan producers contributed perhaps 2 million pounds. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that our butter surplus today is 90 million pounds? Where did 80 million pounds of that surplus come from? It came from Quebec. Why should I support this kind of dairy program? We should have a proper national dairy program. If he had sense, the minister would have stayed here to listen to me. I spoke to him during the dinner hour and he knew that I was going to contribute to the debate. But he could not care less. However, I know he will read my speech, or his assistants will.
Why should we have to transport that butter from Quebec to western Canada and on into British Columbia, where there is a 28 million pounds deficit? Why should we pay the freight on it? Who in B.C. is going to get milk from Quebec? Nobody. Why should we have to get butter from New Zealand? Does that make sense? Is this the type of dairy policy toward which we are headed? Earlier I said that I did not know whether we should scrap the program or the Canadian Dairy Commission.

speechtext: Scrap the government.

I think we should scrap them both. They deserve every credit for trying, but having tried they have failed. These people at the lower end of the ladder are still going to deliver cream. They have delivered it, and they will continue to deliver it. Many of these people are trying to diversify their operations. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) is one of the greatest guys in the world for encouraging diversification. My own minister from Saskatchewan tells me we have to do these things. Mr. Speaker, what do we have to do? The government denies us every opportunity; but later they will regret it.
It was all right when some of the friends of separatism came to this House from Quebec. I am not suggesting for one moment that we in the west will separate. I think we have more guts out there than a lot of people who said they would separate. We are going to stay in Canada. We are going to fight for our rights in Canada. I only hope the minister will listen to reason and put the policy on a regional basis.
On January 21 last, the president of the National Dairy Council of Canada stated:
-the experience of the past few years has demonstrated all too clearly and unhappily the failure in the administration of national policy to recognize and provide the necessary flexibility to cope with the inherent regional differences in the structure and economics of the enterprise.
I am talking not only of western Canada; I am talking about the maritimes and the eastern townships of Quebec. I am not talking provincially; I am talking in terms of whole regions. The government must realize that if it is to solve the problems of transportation and storage, we must call a spade a spade. Where is the surplus developing? It is right here in central Canada. Why should the producers in Saskatchewan have to pay for this when people in other areas are creating the surplus? But we have pulled in our horns. Every province except Quebec has pulled in its horns. Quebec has increased its production. Is this going to continue at our expense? Somebody has to call a spade a spade and I am not too shy to do so.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in this debate tonight. It would seem, from the number of people in the gallery, that the dairy industry in the province of Quebec must be in a very grim state indeed, because it has caused all these visitors to make the trek to Ottawa to listen to this debate. I do not believe people would become involved in the expense of forming such a large delegation just for fun. They must have legitimate problems, otherwise they would not be here. I believe it is significant, also, that many of these people have chosen members from parties other than the two old-line parties to represent them, because in the past they have been unable to achieve the kind of success they desired through those members. They have chosen, instead, to seek spokesmen from outside the two old-line parties.
The dairy farmers in my area are not affected greatly one way or another by the subsidy on milk, but I do not think it follows from that that they have no sympathy for the people who are so affected. I am told the dairy farmers in the province of Quebec depend for at least 25 per cent of their return on this particular subsidy. It also seems a tragedy to me that at a time when two-thirds of the people in the world go to bed hungry, we should have a minister who would stand up here and express concern about the surplus of various food products in this country. There are 3.5 billion people in the world today. In 25 years it is expected there will be 7 billion people. In terms of the hungry people of the world, we cannot begin to feed the people on the earth today. We might ask ourselves whether there will be a surplus in three or four years from now in wheat and dairy products. I do not think this is a longterm problem if we can find a means of providing these commodities to the people of the world who really need them.
Earlier this afternoon we had a prolonged debate in the House about the inability of Canada to feed some starving Metis people. Some of the grain farmers of Saskatchewan had offered to grind flour to help feed these people. We have surpluses in many products. Where are the surplus food products, so far as these Metis people are concerned? They do not exist. We cannot really begin to feed the
February 19, 1970

Government Dairy Policy people we have in. Canada, despite the surpluses. What are we doing about the hungry people of the world? Our record in foreign aid is pitiful if not shocking. What does it matter if we sell milk powder at 6 cents a pound when the world price is 20 cents a pound? This is a way in which Canada could make a contribution to the under-developed countries of the world.
A previous speaker spoke about the deliberate long-term policy to move people off the land. This is a policy designed to make it impossible for them to live in the rural areas and maintain a decent standard of living. Certainly, the problem is one of oversupply-the very problem the Canadian Dairy Commission was set up to solve. It failed. Why, Mr. Speaker? I suggest it failed simply because it was forced to adopt the Liberal concept of bigness. It was compelled to develop policies and programs that cater only to the big operator.
The natural corollary of building bigness is the destruction of smallness; in this instance the destruction of the small producer in the dairy industry. This general policy may be seen in every aspect of the departmental work carried out under the direction of the Minister of Agriculture and his part-time, academic assistant from Saskatoon-Humboldt (Mr. Lang). I recall clearly the statements of the Canadian Dairy Commission and the minister that farmers producing less than 420 pounds of butterfat could not be considered as being serious about the dairy industry. What do we find has happened? Harsh impositions have been applied in an attempt to eliminate those people from the industry.
Again we witnessed a build-up of the big in order to make them bigger and in order to destroy the small and get rid of the inconvenient individual. This, Mr. Speaker, has resulted in the elimination of subsidy to 20,000

When it is claimed that I kneel before the Minister of Agriculture, or when I try sometimes to report on articles signed by Pierre Courtaud and that I am supposed to have said that I am pleased with the minister's decision, then I open a report from the Committee on Agriculture and I try to figure out when I was

He then pointed out that, for the current year, $45 million would be used for marketing dairy products and that, when the Treasury Board grants $125 million to the Canadian Dairy Commission, 94 per cent of the population think that this goes to the farmers when, actually, they only receive 70 per cent. It was in this connection that the Minister said: We must change our capitals. He even disclosed some ideas from the program he was to bring forward. subsubtopic: TRADE-EFFECT OF ENTRY OF GREAT BRITAIN INTO COMMON MARKET ON CANADIAN AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 12 last, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) what explanations himself and the cabinet could give about Great Britain's eventual entry in the Common Market and the repercussions on farm products exports from Canada to Great Britain.
We want to notify the Prime Minister early enough to prevent him from saying that he was not aware of the problem. We want to warn him of the fact that Great Britain, to which during the war, we sold much milk and other agricultural products-which enabled them to win the war and enjoy freedom-will soon enter in the Common Market.
Since Canada exports great quantities of milk powder and cheddar cheese, as we were told by members of the Catholic Farmers Union or any other organization, other difficulties could arise.
In Great Britain, a white paper was published on this topic. The Prime Minister recently met his counterpart from Great Britain. The latter stated this at a press conference before leaving by plane for New York, and I quote:
-that his government was aware of the problems created in Canada by Great Britain's entry in the European Economic Community. "We know the resultant difficulties for our trade partners".-
He added the following:
We know that Great Britain will likely become the seventh member of the E.E.C. in 1970. This economic alliance with Europe should restrain greatly Canadian agricultural exports to England. At the present time our country constitutes the main outlet for Canadian tobacco and agricultural products, such as potatoes-[DOT]
-and pork.
If the Canadian government does not immediately make the necessary representations to Great Britain, in view of the fact that it is a country to which we have rendered great services, and if England does not concern itself with those problems, 25,000 farmers and not only 300 like today will lay siege to the Canadian Parliament to demand justice.
I am urging the government to make representations to the government of Great Britain. One may read the following in the February 11 issue of the Devoir, and I quote:
London-The British Treasury is considering the possibility of refunding before the end of the year all Britain's international short-term debts.
February 19, 1970

As I was trying to explain earlier, since Canada has extended so much help to that country, I am sure that if our Prime Minister or any other minister would start discussing straight away the possibility of maintaining our agricultural imports, we might be able to avoid the very serious problems which will confront us at the end of the year unless the government takes the necessary steps.
That is the reason why I had asked this question which deals with a very urgent problem and I urge the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and also the Minister of Agriculture to send right away some officials to meet the responsible people who are aware of the problems in store for Canada, if they want to avoid a disaster for Canadian agriculture.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not easy to state in three minutes the effect that Great Britain's entry into the Common Market will have on Canada's agricultural exports. One would have to compare tariffs to be applied to Great Britain and to the Common Market countries, although it is not yet known under what conditions Great Britain will finally join the group, as the Prime Minister stated some time ago.
This point having been taken care of, I have a few comments to make. First of all, we have not yet had the opportunity to study the White Paper, for the very good reason that we have not yet received it. We shall study it at the earliest opportunity.
Then, we are well aware of the volume of agricultural exports from Canada to the United Kingdom and of the fact that negotiations have taken place since 1961 on that matter. Recently, a discussion took place in Ottawa between officials of the United Kingdom and Canada. At the last meeting between the Prime Ministers of the two countries, the matter was discussed.
Agricultural exports represent approximately 25 per cent of total exports of $2,1 billion. Wheat accounts for some $105 million, cheese for $15 million and tobacco for $49 million. They are consequently extremely important products.
What will happen if Great Britain joins the common market? That is anybody's guess.
As far as wheat is concerned, we know the common market's protectionist policy, particularly for agricultural products.
Canada is now exporting as much wheat to common market countries as to England.


If Canada manages to export some into the common market now, it is most likely that she shall continue to do so when England has joined it.
The minister without portofolio in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) discussed recently with English buyers who were quite optimistic about the future of this kind of export.
As regards cheddar cheese, the situation will deteriorate since the free access we enjoy to England, the preferential treatment we are accorded by her, not only will be lost but the Common Market members will themselves enjoy it for this product.
On the other hand, since a transitory period will certainly take place following England's entry into the common market, it is possible that we might convince the Europeans themselves of the good quality of Canadian cheese.
In any case, the United Kingdom and the Common Market are well aware of our concern in this regard. We are insisting, have insisted and will insist with the British, as the Prime Minister has said before, on an exchange of views before during and after negotiations. subsubtopic: NATIONAL CAPITAL-REQUEST FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 13, as recorded at page 2305 of Hansard, I posed a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in respect of the unapprecialive attitude of the city of Ottawa. I asked:
-will the Prime Minister give serious consideration to decentralizing federal civil servants by moving government departments to the west and to the maritime provinces in order to give those areas a shot in the arm, so to speak?
At that particular time my intention really was to draw the attention of the government to the fact that there was a dispute between the government and the city of Ottawa. My colleague from Surrey (Mr. Mather) made that point very well in a previous question when he asked whether the Prime Minister would consider implementing the decision of the previous Parliament and encourage the establishment of a committee of Parliament to deal with all matters pertaining to the national capital.
February 19, 1970

The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) suggested that this could be done at an early date. It would appear to me from some of the correspondence I have received since this question was asked that many people in Ottawa, particularly some in the municipal government, do not realize the benefit that is derived from a federal civil service payroll such as there is in this city. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, whether or not the federal government tries to treat the city council of Ottawa as a small brother, I do not believe this is really the point. If they do, then the revitalization of the committee about which the hon. member spoke is most urgent.
I would suggest there is great merit in taking into consideration some decentralization of our federal departments. I can think of some points to which these departments might be moved. What better place would there be than Moose Jaw for the Department of Agriculture? I would think in that area the department would be close to the troubes affecting many people of this nation. I believe the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) would be only too pleased to move his office to the constituency of the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner). I am sure such a move would be appreciated by the people in that area.
I believe one point we should remember is that a civil service payroll in any city is one of the most important items to any government whether municipal or provincial. The fact remains that whether or not we decentralize our civil service payroll so that it is smaller in the city of Ottawa is a matter about which all of us should be concerned. If the city of Ottawa believes an industrial payroll is more important than a civil service payroll, it should say so.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Let us decentralize the departments and locate them in areas of Canada where they can be closer to the action that is developing.
I well remember the time last summer when the then member of the legislative assembly of British Columbia, Bill King, the member for Revelstoke-Slocan, wrote to the Prime Minister asking him to locate the forestry department in Revelstoke. I thought it was an excellent idea and that this was a good place for locating the department.
What better place could there be for locating the new Arctic department of the Department of Transport which is now being reorganized, than the Arctic? The minister said he plans to do this and I give him due credit

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion for it. At the same time, I believe it is most important when we consider decentralization-if the government is sincere about it-to try to place the departments of the government in those areas of Canada which will give all people of Canada a voice in our federal government.
A few years back it was argued that communications would be the main stumbling block, but all of us know today that under the capable hands of the Department of Communications it is no stumbling-block. We can have more or less instantaneous communication with any area of Canada through satellites and other means. There is no reason to say that we have to be close to the seat of government to be able to communicate with the rest of Canada.
I believe the government should give serious consideration to decentralization so as to give all the people of Canada a say in the federal government, for which they are paying and in which they should have a part.
