EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-APPLICATION RESPECTING FLOODING OF LAND NEAR SKAGIT RIVER
speechtext:
Before I start, Mr. Speaker, I should say that the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Pringle) attempted to get your eye earlier today. However, I was fortunate in getting it and he was not, so I happen to be speaking tonight rather than him.
The question I raised of the Skagit Valley is one of increasing concern to British Columbians and indeed to all Canadians concerned with conservation. I should like to briefly outline the sequence of events. In January, 1942, the International Joint Commission granted a permit to the city of Seattle to erect the Ross dam on the Skagit River in the United States. The upper end of the lake formed by this dam extended a quarter of a mile into Canada. In this 1942 agreement provision was made for a second and subsequent agreement which would further raise the height of the dam and further extend the lake into Canada.
In 1957 there was a hearing in Ottawa at which the second agreement was considered, but at that time no such agreement resulted. If my information is correct, these hearings came to naught and it was only in 1957 that there was a second agreement entered into between the province of British Columbia on the one hand and the city of Seattle on the other. This agreement called for a further flooding of some 5,800 acres of land for the payment of approximately $34,500 to the province of British Columbia-some $5.50 per acre.
IMr. O'Connell.]
DEBATES	February 19, 1970
Mr. Speaker, if the matter stood there perhaps there would be no cause for me or for the hon. member for Fraser Valley East to raise it in this House and express our concern. But there is another factor which must be mentioned, and that is, in 1955 the federal government passed the International River Improvements Act which states in section 4:
No person shall construct, operate or maintain an international river improvement unless he holds a valid licence therefor issued under this act.
"International river improvement" as defined in section 2 means:
-a dam, obstruction, canal, reservoir or other work the purpose or effect of which is (i) to increase, decrease or alter the natural flow of an international river-
Therefore, it appears that in 1955 the situation was materially altered and the federal government acquired complete control by this act. I might add, Mr. Speaker, that the purpose of the act was to protect the people of British Columbia from the folly and greed of the provincial government of the day on the Libby dam question, which is not dissimilar to the Skagit affair.
My question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) earlier today was whether an application under the International River Improvements Act has been received from the city of Seattle by the federal government, and whether the minister has accepted or rejected any such application. Perhaps if I read a few lines from the Newsletter of the Federation of British Columbia Naturalists Your Honour will understand why I regard it as very important for any application by the city of Seattle to be most carefully examined by the federal government. This Newsletter is dated December 9, 1969, and reads as follows:
Fishing values are also very high-it is said that as many as 6,000 are in there at times for the fishing. The loss of spawning beds with consequent decline in later years of fishing quality is probably the greatest adverse effect the damming will have but loss of most of the wider part of the valley is also important as this is a readily accessible area for the heavily populated coast area.
The narrow valley of the Skagit to the northeast is uncut for about six miles and is under reserve by the forest service as a buffer zone along the river. Under the circumstances should this ever be lifted as it is an exceptionally beautiful valley, the fishing is excellent in the river, and the old gold miner's access trail from the U.S. runs up the river on the east side and is still in good condition.
I should like to say a word, finally, in describing why this valley is important and why this is a matter of urgency at this time,
February 19, 1970

which perhaps earlier today Your Honour was not able to fully understand. Only a few days ago in the B.C. Gazette bids were called for the cutting of timber in this valley. There can be no doubt from the statements of the provincial minister of resources, Mr. Ray Wil-liston, as quoted in the Province and Sun of February 11 and 12, that this invitation to bid is to clear the valley of timber, to destroy its fishing and recreational value in anticipation of further flooding for which no permit has been granted by the federal government.
It is most important for the federal government to make clear now that it will examine the application of Seattle City Power, when it comes, on its merits and that this crude attempt to destroy the resources of the valley and its value in the area will have no effect whatsoever on the decision of the federal government. We must point out very clearly that an attempt at a scorched earth policy is about to be made on the Skagit Valley; this will not lead us to decide that the valley is worthless and that we can, therefore, grant a permit to raise the dam and flood this area.
It is for these reasons, Mr. Speaker, that I regard this as a most urgent and important matter and raise it tonight.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to acknowledge the forthright submission of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Anderson) and recognize that the other part of the pincer is the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Pringle) who was not able to catch Mr. Speaker's eye this afternoon. The Ross dam was built by Seattle Light and Power, now taken over by the city of Seattle, on the Skagit River in the state of Washington to meet part of the city's electrical power requirements.
The dam was built to raise the water level of the Skagit River to an elevation of about 1,600 feet above mean sea level. At this level the reservoir reaches the international boundary; but there is no appreciable backwater extending into the province of British Columbia. When the reservoir is absolutely full, a maximum of possibly 5 to 10 acres of British Columbia land is under water at 2 feet or less in depth. The Ross Dam was built with the intention of its being raised ultimately by 125 feet, which would extend the

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion reservoir into British Columbia when the water reached the new maximum level of about 1,725 feet.
Nearly 40 years ago the city of Seattle acquired ownership of virtually all the approximately 640 acres of privately-owned land that would be flooded with the reservoir filled to the 1,725 feet level. The remaining area of British Columbia that would be flooded is about 5,710 acres of land owned by the Crown in right of the province. In preparation for this future construction to raise the Ross dam to the 1,725 feet level, the city of Seattle made application which resulted in the issuing by the International Joint Commission of an order of approval on January 27, 1942. This order of approval contained a condition that the city of Seattle must arrive at a mutually acceptable agreement with the province of British Columbia to cover the damages caused to British Columbia by the raising of the Ross dam.
On January 10, 1967, British Columbia and Seattle Light and Power reached an agreement. However, this was never formalized. In 1955, a new element of the situation had been introduced with passage by Parliament of the International River Improvements Act. The city of Seattle has not yet applied for a licence or an exception under the In' ernation-al River Improvements Act, which provides a requirement for such licence or exception to cover a work which has the effect of changing the water level at the international boundary by more than one-tenth of a foot. The city of Seattle has not begun any of the construction required to raise the Ross dam to result in a level of 1,725 feet. It is understood that the city of Seattle also must obtain a new or amended licence from the United States Federal Power Commission to permit the flooding of land in the United States.
In conclusion may I say that, naturally, the government of Canada would want to be assured that any agreement between the British Columbia government and Seattle Light and Power Authority would be in accordance with the IJC statement of 1942. In all probability as well, public hearings will be called for by the government, particularly since we recognize the fundamental rights of Canadians living in British Columbia.
